title: eKlinika — Iđirot (Acorus calamus)
summary: Uses Temišvarka as a common name for the wetland plant iđirot/Acorus calamus, illustrating the dominant non-grape meaning returned by targeted searches.
notes: This source does not by itself disprove an undocumented folk grape name; the negative conclusion rests on its combination with VIVC, wein.plus, CEVVIN and scientific silence.

title: Vinograd.info — Креаца, Банат Рислинг
summary: Lists Kreaca/Banat Riesling forms and gives 16–18% sugar, but calls the cultivar early-middle or middle ripening, conflicting with CEVVIN, the 1964 manual and Croatian Vinopedia.
notes: The page does not expose a primary source for all agronomic statements, so the stronger Serbian technical consensus retains priority while the conflict is preserved.

title: Vinopedia — Vojvodina
summary: Treats Kreaca/Banatski rizling as a local Vojvodina cultivar and places it among late-ripening grapes, independently supporting the regional identity and timing.
notes: This is not Croatian Wikipedia and supplies no current Drašković blend or tasting profile.

title: Dimiat
summary: Treats Smederevka as a synonym of Bulgarian Dimyat, calls the cultivar white, large-berried and potentially high-yielding, gives current Serbian rank/region figures and describes Dimyat wines as light-bodied but very aromatic. It does not verify the exact analysis, king-of-spritzer nickname, dilution mechanism, CEVVIN attribution or current Biser.
notes: Its aromatic claim directly prevents an unqualified universal «neutral» label. Origin and Serbian area percentages should be checked against current CEVVIN rather than the article's older snapshots.

title: Dimiat
summary: Identifies Smederevka/Smederevka bijela/white and Szemendriai forms among Dimiat synonyms. The article gives no Serbian analytical pair, spritzer claim, CEVVIN sparkling assessment, market-use quantification or Biser tasting.
notes: Its main value is identity/synonym cross-checking; detailed Serbian claims require current national and product sources.

title: Fröccs; no detailed Smederevka article
provenance: Hungarian Wikipedia beverage article and targeted Smederevka search
summary: Hungarian Wikipedia provides rich soda-wine ratio terminology but no comparable Smederevka/Dimyat cultivar profile or support for calling the grape «king of spritzer». Its many ratios also show that dilution practice is not one fixed formula.
notes: Useful for cultural comparison only; it does not verify Serbian sensory or analytical claims.

title: Шприцер; без профила Смедеревке
provenance: Serbian Wikipedia beverage article and targeted cultivar search
summary: Defines Serbian špricer narrowly as white wine with siphon soda and distinguishes gemišt with mineral water, but has no sourced Smederevka article, analytical profile, nickname or sparkling-wine evidence.
notes: The short article itself lacks robust citations, so producer and national sources carry more weight even for usage.

title: Шприцер и виноделие в Сербии; без профиля Смедеревки
provenance: Russian Wikipedia beverage article cross-checked with its Serbia wine overview
summary: Defines a wine-and-carbonated-water spritzer and treats 1:1 as a classic rather than mandatory ratio. Russian Wikipedia lists Smederevka in Serbia but supplies no cultivar descriptors, exact analysis, nickname, sparkling potential or Biser.
notes: The Russian spritzer page is weakly sourced and cannot establish Smederevka-specific dilution performance.

title: Gemišt; nema posebnog profila Smederevke
provenance: Croatian Wikipedia beverage article and targeted cultivar search
summary: Defines gemišt as dry white wine plus carbonated mineral water in variable proportions and distinguishes Serbian špricer with soda; no Smederevka technical or sensory profile was found.
notes: Terminology is useful but cannot prove the book's nickname or acid-retention mechanism.

title: CEVVIN — Smederevka cultivar profile
provenance: Serbian Centre for Viticulture and Winemaking cultivar/register profile
summary: Calls Smederevka a very old Serbian/Balkan white grown widely across the Balkans, high-yielding, early-starting and very late-ripening, frost-sensitive and capable of must acidity around 9 g/L when high yield suppresses sugar. Wine is light, drinkable and pleasantly aromatic, sometimes vanilla-like; the grape is used to correct acidity in blends and widely eaten fresh. It ranks 12th, led by South Banat, Three Moravas and Šumadija.
notes: The public page does not mention sparkling wine, the exact 6.83/10.5 pair or «king of spritzer»; attributing sparkling potential directly to CEVVIN therefore requires the separate publication that the book appears to paraphrase.

title: NIN — Smederevka: Indigenous, timeless, and uniquely its own
provenance: Serbian national magazine summarising CEVVIN and modern winemaking
summary: Describes Smederevka as high-yielding and Balkan-wide, with light, fresh, drinkable, crisp wines; lemon, herbs, white flowers, vanillin and spices; good acidity, frequent soda use and suitability for sparkling wine. It notes increasing experimentation and unfulfilled overall potential.
notes: Popular synthesis rather than a technical sheet; superlatives and broad renaissance claims are downweighted.

title: Ivanova-Petropulos et al. — Influence of variety and vintage on Smederevka and Vranec wines
provenance: Original peer-reviewed six-vintage physicochemical study using OIV methods
summary: For Smederevka wines from Ovče Pole, 2018–2023, reports alcohol 10.21–11.0%, total acidity 4.8–7.2 g/L and means 10.8%/5.74 g/L. It supports moderate alcohol and fresh acidity but does not reproduce the book's exact paired 6.83/10.5 analysis.
notes: North Macedonian single-protocol results should not be universalised to all Serbian wines.

title: Rubin — Smederevka
provenance: Current primary product record captured in public index
summary: Documents a current Rubin Smederevka at 10.5% alcohol and describes freshness, but gives no total-acidity value.
notes: The page's current anti-bot interstitial limits direct text access; the public indexed product facts were preserved earlier in the audit.

title: Vinarija Mišić — Smederevka
provenance: Primary product page from Smederevsko vinogorje
summary: Describes a light-yellow dry table white with pleasant aroma and refreshing taste and says its sharper fresh note makes it widely used for cold summer špricer in Serbia.
notes: Producer marketing supports strong cultural association but not the exact nickname or a comparative dilution mechanism.

title: Robinson et al. — Interactions between wine volatile compounds and matrix components
provenance: Peer-reviewed Journal of Agricultural and Food Chemistry study
summary: Shows that water, ethanol and other matrix components alter volatile release and perception in complex ways; dilution cannot be reduced to a Smederevka-specific rule that acidity alone preserves the wine better.
notes: No comparative Smederevka spritzer sensory experiment was found.

title: Vinarija Aleksić — Biser
summary: Lists Biser as current 100% Smederevka sparkling wine made by the traditional method at 12% alcohol. The producer note gives straw yellow-green colour, very lively freshness, dried flowers, yellow-apple skin and warm-croissant hints.
notes: Producer sensory description is cross-checked against Falstaff; the current page does not state vintage, dosage or time on lees.

title: Falstaff — Aleksić Biser Extra Brut 2016
provenance: Independent Falstaff tasting by Peter Moser, 2022
summary: Catalogues the 2016 as Smederevka, 11.5% alcohol and 91 points. The note gives lively mousse, white stone fruit, lime zest, biscuit, green apple, medium body, fresh acidity and a mineral-citrus finish.
notes: The tasting proves one successful release and current product continuity is established separately; it does not quantify national market share.

title: wein.plus public Wine Guide and lexicon search — Smederevka
provenance: User-requested specialist database; public/free material only
summary: The unobscured public index did not yield a specific Serbian Smederevka cultivar or wine card that independently verifies this block or adds a current missing object.
notes: No Premium, blurred or restricted text was extracted and no access control was bypassed.

title: SerbianWine.rs — Smederevka overview
summary: Calls Smederevka/Dimyat a historic regional white that generally makes fresh, straightforward wines served young. It supplies no exact analysis, agronomic profile, spritzer mechanism, sparkling example or Biser descriptor set.
notes: The page's cautious historical wording is more reliable than treating Serbian or Bulgarian origin as finally settled.

title: Dobro Jutro — Stare autohtone sorte grožđa: Smederevka
provenance: Serbian agricultural reference reproducing an ampelographic technical profile
summary: Gives 14–25 t/ha, neutral colourless must at 16–20% sugar and 7–9 g/L acids, and wine at 9–11% alcohol and 6–8 g/L acids. Wine is refreshing, harmonious and varietally scented; it is used for acid correction, brandy, sparkling wine and fresh consumption.
notes: Secondary reproduction without a clearly visible original monograph citation; CEVVIN and peer-reviewed measurements take priority where values differ.

title: Falstaff — Smederevka grape variety
provenance: International wine reference and tasting database
summary: Treats Smederevka as Dimyat, late-ripening, winter-frost vulnerable, high-yielding and often sold as table grapes. It calls the wines rather neutral and notes sparkling use due to fresh acidity; its catalogue contains both Belina and Aleksić Biser.
notes: Its Bulgarian-origin framing conflicts with Serbian autochthonous narratives; the card is used for identity and traits, not national ownership.

title: Vino.rs — Beograđani spasavaju smederevku
provenance: Serbian specialist report on Vinarija Emporio
summary: Documents a mature elegant brut sparkling wine associated with Emporio and quotes the producer's strong assessment of Smederevka for sparkling production, supplying another concrete use beyond Biser.
notes: The report does not provide a full technical sheet or current-vintage status, so Emporio remains a historical/portfolio counterexample rather than proof of broad market share.

title: Kadarka
summary: Identifies Kadarka/Cadarca/Gamza as one Balkan–Central European red variety and records a proposed Papazkarasi parent. Its description of medium-dark or dark, deeply aromatic wine conflicts with the book's pale-colour generalization; it does not establish the Serbian migration date, exact descriptor list, synonym count or Prokupac parentage.
notes: Highest-priority Wikipedia by requested language ranking, but its sensory paragraph is weakly sourced and should not override genetics, official synonymy or current specialist evidence.

title: Kadarka
summary: Describes very thin-skinned berries, high rot tendency, late ripening and lightly spicy grapes, yet says successful monovarietal wines can be dark, tannic, extract-rich and age well. It therefore supports skin and disease traits while contradicting a universal pale, medium-bodied style.
notes: The article's origin claim differs from EN and other sources; exact fruit descriptors, migration century and modern genetics are absent.

title: Kadarka
summary: Presents Kadarka as an aromatic, spicy and historically important Hungarian-region variety whose wine style varies with site, including lighter, fresher expressions on sand. It does not provide robust evidence for the book's exact fruit list, two-to-three-year rule, direct Prokupac ancestry or one migration century.
notes: Culturally relevant but not independent evidence that the cultivar is genetically Hungarian; official Hungarian wine communication is preferred for current national framing.

title: Кадарка
summary: Describes an elegant, light, harmonious and cherry-led style with moderate acidity and acknowledges stylistic diversity. It does not substantiate prominent tannin, the exact oak-derived descriptors, synonym count, direct genetic relationship or precise migration date.
notes: Useful for Serbian terminology but subordinate to CEVVIN, peer-reviewed genetics and primary product pages.

title: Кадарка
summary: Defines Kadarka as a black wine grape, lists Gamza and Četereška among synonyms and describes dark-blue berries with thin skin. It supplies almost no reliable sensory, ageing, genetic or migration analysis.
notes: Sparse sourcing makes the official EU synonym list, CEVVIN and genetics more authoritative.

title: Kadarka
summary: Describes ruby, aromatic, soft and fresh medium-bodied wine and provides regional identity context. It does not verify the detailed fruit and barrel notes, exact ageing window, synonym total, genetics or migration century.
notes: Supports the centre of the book's style but not every descriptor or causal statement.

title: Commission communication — grape variety names and synonyms
summary: The regulatory name list maps Kadarka to Csetereska and Gamza and contains the relevant regional name tradition; it confirms legal synonym use without endorsing sensory or historical claims.
notes: National spellings and diacritics vary; this source is stronger than Wikipedia for identity but is not a complete VIVC synonym passport.

title: wein.plus Lexicon — Kadarka
provenance: Publicly visible specialist wine lexicon entry
summary: Reports around 150 synonyms and publicly lists Gamza, Branicevka and Skadarka among country-grouped names. The visible excerpt confirms Balkan identity and synonym scale but does not supply the book's sensory, ageing or migration details.
notes: Only openly displayed text was used; no Premium text, blur recovery or access-control circumvention was attempted.

title: RTS — Srpska kadarka, gotovo zaboravljena, može da zameni i svetske sorte grožđa
provenance: Serbian public broadcaster report with grower and sommelier quotations
summary: Confirms Braničevka/Četereška and Bulgarian Gamza, Subotica importance, low colouring matter, cherry, raspberry, sweet cherry, spice, acidity and freshness. It does not mention plum, wild rose or a two-to-three-year maturation rule.
notes: Some historical claims originate with interviewed producers; analytical and genetic conclusions require stronger sources.

title: Vino & Fino — Kadarka, drevna sorta za budućnost
provenance: Serbian specialist wine magazine variety feature
summary: Describes late ripening, Botrytis and frost sensitivity, delicately coloured wines, red and black cherry, cranberry, plum, raspberry, strawberry, pepper/spice, fresh fine acidity, moderate body and soft tannin. It says good complex Kadarka may age beyond a decade and treats Balkan-to-Hungary history as a hypothesis.
notes: General varietal prose synthesizes other wine literature; it supports occurrence and range, not mandatory descriptors in every bottle.

title: Magyar Bor — Kadarka
summary: Calls Kadarka pale, elegant, fresh and low-tannin, with low anthocyanins, red berries, cherry, fresh spice, paprika, gingerbread, herbs and delicate floral notes. It frames the style as light to medium-bodied, recommends young consumption within one or two years, and explicitly says the variety is not Hungarian in origin but is now considered Hungarian/local to the Carpathian Basin.
notes: Promotional national source; very useful for current Hungarian self-definition but not proof of ancient origin or migration date.

title: Dukay Winery — 2021 Dukay Kadarka
provenance: Official product page for the apparent source of the card's base descriptors
summary: Describes ruby red colour, Kadarka spice, raspberry, currant and plum, a tight acid backbone, freshness and elegant fullness; gives 11.5% alcohol, 5.2 g/L acid and nine months maturation.
notes: Machine-rendered English can blur currant colour and stylistic nuance; the Hungarian original is used to check terminology. One bottle cannot define the cultivar universally.

title: Dukay Winery — Kadarka Reserve 2020
provenance: Official producer portfolio in Hungarian and English
summary: Describes an unusually deeper-red Kadarka Reserve matured in oak, with special spice, csipkebogyó (rosehip), cherry, rounded acidity and creamy fruit.
notes: The book's «дикая роза» mistranslates Hungarian csipkebogyó; it is rosehip. The evidence is a specific Reserve, not plural oak versions or proof that oak causes cherry.

title: The genetic characterization of grapevines prospected in old Serbian vineyards reveals multiple relationships between traditional varieties of the Balkans
provenance: Peer-reviewed Frontiers in Plant Science study, DOI 10.3389/fpls.2024.1391679
summary: Places both cultivars in a broad Balkan diversity study, identifies Prokupac as founder of a multigenerational lineage, but separately finds Kadarka SRB parent–offspring related to Heunisch Weiss. It does not report direct Prokupac–Kadarka parentage.
notes: The study also warns about identity corrections in old germplasm; broad clustering must not be rewritten as a specific pedigree.

title: wein.plus Lexicon — Papazkarasi
provenance: Public specialist lexicon entry summarizing 2013 DNA analysis
summary: States that Papazkarasi is a presumed natural Alba Imputotato × Prokupac cross. Some popular Kadarka narratives then make Papazkarasi a Kadarka parent, which would make Prokupac an indirect ancestor, but this page itself does not establish the second link.
notes: Only public text used. The chain is a composite hypothesis and conflicts with newer Kadarka–Heunisch first-degree evidence unless accession identity or pedigree interpretation is resolved.

title: Association de la Sommellerie Internationale — Host Serbia grape overview
summary: Lists Skadarka, Braničevka, Gmza, Mekiš and Četereška as Kadarka names and says the variety moved north during the Great Migration of the Serbs, without giving a rigorous cultivar-specific date.
notes: The Serbia-host text likely draws on national promotional material; it is not an independent archival history.

title: CEVVIN — Skadarka
provenance: Serbian Center for Viticulture and Winemaking national variety profile
summary: Lists Kadarka, Četereska and Branicevka as Skadarka synonyms, calls it Balkan, says it moved into the Pannonian plain during an eighteenth-century northward migration, and identifies Subotica, Srem and Negotinska Krajina as its largest Serbian areas. It also reports compact bunches and great susceptibility to grey mould.
notes: Its eighteenth-century date directly conflicts with the book's seventeenth century and the Great Migration tradition; the profile does not cite an archival document for the date.

title: What do we know about grapevine bunch compactness? A state-of-the-art review
provenance: Peer-reviewed Australian Journal of Grape and Wine Research review
summary: Concludes that compact grape bunches are more susceptible to Botrytis bunch rot and explains that bunch density, berry traits, genotype, environment and management jointly affect sanitary risk.
notes: Not Kadarka-specific; it qualifies the book's single-cause thin-skin explanation rather than replacing cultivar observations.

title: Fermentation temperature and duration effect on the quality and anthocyanin content of Kadarka wine produced in the Miniș wine region
summary: Shows that Kadarka wine anthocyanin content changes with fermentation temperature and maceration duration, with a reported maximum under one tested regime. This supports vinification-dependent colour and does not demonstrate skin thinness as the sole cause of paleness.
notes: One region and experiment; it does not establish the population-wide pigment range or preferred style.

title: SerbianWine.rs — current indigenous-grape overview
summary: The current indigenous-grape overview has no Kadarka/Skadarka section and therefore provides no direct verification of this card's identity, descriptors, genetics or history.
notes: No hidden, blurred or Premium material was used. Separate SerbianWine.rs winery anomalies involving a purported Bikicki Kadarka were already recorded in G0058 and remain unverified.

title: Kadarka; Rakovac Monastery
summary: Provides general Kadarka history, decline and regional distribution and separately identifies Rakovac Monastery on Fruška Gora. It contains none of the Serbian 11.60-ha inventory, named-producer market count, Fruška Gora 60%/two-thirds figures or Bolić priority claim.
notes: English Wikipedia has highest requested Wikipedia priority, but local statistics and the historical book require primary or Serbian specialist sources.

title: Kadarka; Kloster Rakovac — deutschsprachige Wikipedia und Suche
summary: Notes broad decline of Kadarka plantings and demanding cultivation but gives no Serbian area, market list, Fruška Gora historic share or Bolić bibliographic evidence.
notes: No sufficiently detailed German article on Bolić was found.

title: Kadarka; Tarcal-hegység; Prokopije Bolić — magyar Wikipédia keresés
summary: Gives extensive Hungarian Kadarka history and decline but no verifiable Serbian 2019 area, current producer list, Fruška Gora historic denominator or Bolić first-record evidence.
notes: Hungarian nationwide 60% traditions must not be silently transferred to Fruška Gora.

title: Кадарка; манастир Раковац; Прокопије Болић — српска Википедија и претрага
summary: Supplies general local Kadarka background but not the 2019 commercial-area figure, producer enumeration, 60%/two-thirds historical fractions or a sourced proof that Bolić 1816 was the first written trace.
notes: CEVVIN and the 2024 genetics/history paper are preferred for the local claims.

title: Кадарка; монастырь Раковац; Прокопий Болич — русская Википедия и поиск
summary: The short Kadarka article gives only broad distribution and viticulture; no Serbian hectares, wineries, historic Fruška shares, Yugoslav policy evidence or Bolić record is available.
notes: The article cannot verify any of the block's exact numbers or priority claims.

title: Kadarka; manastir Rakovac; Prokopije Bolić — hrvatska Wikipedija i pretraga
summary: Provides general Kadarka description without the Serbian inventory, current estate list, Fruška Gora historic percentage, socialist-displacement documentation or Bolić bibliographic detail.
notes: Regional proximity does not compensate for the absence of cited Serbian data.

title: CEVVIN — Autohtone i regionalne sorte vinove loze Srbije (2019)
provenance: National specialist inventory, Darko Jakšić et al., ISBN 978-86-912489-1-8
summary: Reports 11.60 ha of Kadarka in Serbia's commercial vineyards and aggregate distribution. It demonstrates rarity but does not list owners, current bottlers or reproduce historic Fruška Gora percentages.
notes: The denominator is registered commercial vineyards in 2019, not every garden vine or current 2026 area.

title: Vino.rs — Kadarka, zapostavljeni vinski dragulj Srbije
summary: Says the Serbian market then practically showed Tonković, Sagmeister and Maurer, calls Kadarka formerly dominant on Fruška Gora at about 60% of vineyard area roughly a century earlier, and attributes decline to Yugoslav planting of more productive and economical international cultivars.
notes: No archival census is cited for 60%; the producer list is a 2022 snapshot and already incomplete if every local/table bottling or later entrant is counted.

title: Vino.rs — Kadarka u vrhu najboljih crvenih vina Srbije
summary: Quotes Sagmeister saying Kadarka made up two thirds of Fruška Gora vineyards in the nineteenth century and criticizing socialist-era neglect of economically unattractive varieties.
notes: The quotation accurately supports what Sagmeister said, but not the historical fraction independently; no census or page reference accompanies it.

title: Taste Hungary — Kadarka, Hungary's Answer to Pinot Noir?
summary: Explains post-war socialist decline through a planned-economy preference for volume, mechanization and cultivars better suited to industrial production; Kadarka's rot, frost, uneven ripening and labour needs made it a poor fit.
notes: Hungarian rather than Serbian case; it corroborates the system-level mechanism but cannot quantify Fruška Gora replacement.

title: The genetic characterization of grapevines prospected in old Serbian vineyards reveals multiple relationships between traditional varieties of the Balkans
provenance: Peer-reviewed Frontiers in Plant Science article
summary: States that Bolić in 1816 recorded Skadarka (Kadarka Kek) among cultivars promoted or described for Fruška Gora/Serbian viticulture. It confirms the mention but does not call it the first written trace or rank Skadarka unambiguously among the most important.
notes: A modern scholarly synthesis, not a page image of the 1816 book; exact wording should be checked against a facsimile.

title: Soveršen vinodelac — Prokopije Bolić, 1816
summary: Confirms title, author, Buda 1816 publication and identifies Bolić as archimandrite of Rakovac Monastery; the visible listing does not reproduce the Skadarka entry or prove first mention.
notes: A commercial antiquarian catalogue is acceptable for physical-edition metadata but not a substitute for primary-page transcription.

title: Vino.rs — A kao ampelografija
provenance: Serbian specialist history overview citing Lazić 1982
summary: Says Bolić described 35 Srem cultivars in 1816 with folk names, botanical traits and sometimes economic-technological notes. It establishes the manual's ampelographic scope but not Skadarka priority or exact importance rank.
notes: The article is secondary and should be complemented by a facsimile before quoting historic wording.

title: Vinarija Tonković — current winery and wines
summary: Shows a Kadarka-focused portfolio including Allegro blanc de noirs, Rosé, Fantazija, Rapsodija and other current estate material.
notes: Individual vintage availability and vineyard area can change; the site is primary but promotional.

title: East West Wines — Ernő Sagmeister, Fruška Gora
provenance: Current importer profile and linked wine sheets
summary: Lists Kadarka among Sagmeister's primary Fruška Gora varieties and current vineyard-designated Kadarka releases such as Devas.
notes: Commercial importer; individual wines are independently catalogued by Falstaff elsewhere in the audit.

title: SerbianWine.rs — Oszkar Maurer Winery
summary: Profiles Maurer's Subotica and Fruška Gora vineyards and lists Kadarka, including the 1880 planting, among top products; current Falstaff records independently confirm multiple bottlings.
notes: The page's «Established 1880» field conflates vineyard date with winery history, so only the product and site information is used.

title: wein.plus Lexicon — Kadarka
provenance: Publicly visible specialist wine lexicon entry
summary: The public entry confirms identity and broad Balkan history but contains no Serbian 2019 area, current bottler count, Fruška Gora historical percentage or Bolić priority evidence.
notes: Only public text used; no Premium or obscured content was accessed.

title: Kadarka
summary: Lists Cetereska, Chetereshka, Skadarka and Skadarska among Kadarka synonyms and presents Hungary and a Lake Scutari/Skadarsko connection as competing origin hypotheses. It does not prove Hungarian word formation, Negotin exclusivity or the three-name label claim.
notes: The article's origin field and prose are internally cautious but rely partly on older wine literature; specialist and official sources are preferred for conclusions.

title: Kadarka
summary: Lists Cetereska and Skadarka as Kadarka synonyms and places the cultivar broadly between the Balkans and Hungary, but asserts North Macedonia as an origin without resolving the wider dispute. It gives no name-etymology, Negotin-local or label evidence.
notes: Its origin assertion conflicts with EN, HU and stronger specialist summaries, demonstrating lack of Wikipedia consensus.

title: Kadarka
summary: Calls the cultivar's origin uncertain between Asia Minor and Albania, says the name derives from the Serbo-Croatian name Skadar for Shkodër and says it reached Hungary from the Balkans, probably through Serbian mediation. It does not establish Četereška's Negotin status or a three-label corpus.
notes: The categorical etymological wording is stronger than its evidence warrants and is softened by Wine Grapes and official Hungarian wine material.

title: Кадарка
summary: Provides local Kadarka context but does not independently document the proposed Hungarian-name pathway, Četereška's claimed Negotin exclusivity, a demonstrated Skadar etymology or all three names on labels.
notes: CEVVIN, official synonym lists and historical literature are stronger for Serbian terminology.

title: Кадарка
summary: Lists Скадарка and Четерешка among names of Kadarka but gives no sourced etymology, regional allocation of Četereška or label evidence; its infobox simplistically names Hungary while the prose gives little origin analysis.
notes: Sparse and weakly sourced; useful for Russian terminology only.

title: Kadarka
summary: Gives Kadarka's regional cultivation and historical decline in Vojvodina and Slavonia, but does not supply the three-name synonym argument, a reliable etymology, Negotin name evidence or a label corpus.
notes: Its reporting is largely based on wine journalism and is not decisive on origins.

title: Commission communication — grape variety names and synonyms
summary: Maps Kadarka, Csetereska and Gamza in the regulatory grape-name list, independently confirming that Četereška/Csetereska is a recognized synonym rather than a separate variety.
notes: A legal synonym list does not prove regional exclusivity, etymology or front-label frequency.

title: CEVVIN — Skadarka
provenance: Serbian Center for Viticulture and Winemaking national variety profile
summary: Uses Skadarka as the Serbian profile name, lists Kadarka and Četereska among synonyms, treats the cultivar as probably Balkan and locates major Serbian plantings in Subotica, Srem and Negotinska Krajina. It does not state that Četereška is exclusive to Negotin or prove the Skadar etymology.
notes: The site's protected-copy interface was respected; only publicly rendered/search-visible information was used.

title: wein.plus Lexicon — Kadarka
provenance: Publicly visible specialist wine lexicon entry
summary: Groups Skadarka and related country names under Kadarka and frames the variety within a broad Balkan history. The public entry supports synonym identity but not an exact Skadar derivation or Negotin-label usage.
notes: Only open text was used; no Premium, blurred or otherwise access-controlled content was recovered.

title: Magyar Bor — Kadarka
summary: Says Kadarka is not Hungarian in origin, is probably Balkan and is often associated with Shkodra, while explicitly acknowledging that the exact origin is unknown. It confirms the strength of the Hungarian Kadarka name tradition without proving Hungarian etymology.
notes: National promotional source, checked against independent Wine Grapes synthesis.

title: Hungarianwines.eu — Kadarka in Wine Grapes
provenance: Public excerpt from Robinson, Harding and Vouillamoz, Wine Grapes
summary: Lists Skadarka as a Serbian/Croatian synonym, reports the Serbian-to-Hungary and Scutari-name story as a proposition, and concludes that the exact origin is unknown somewhere in the Balkan–Pannonian area; it also records competing Bulgarian, Romanian and Asia Minor hypotheses.
notes: The excerpt is paraphrased and minimally quoted in the audit; its cited historical literature remains the underlying evidence.

title: RTS — Srpska kadarka, gotovo zaboravljena, može da zameni i svetske sorte grožđa
provenance: Serbian public broadcaster report with grower and sommelier quotations
summary: Uses Braničevka and Četereška as Serbian Kadarka names and discusses the cultivar in Subotica and wider Serbian history. It supports living local usage but not exclusivity to Negotinska Krajina.
notes: Producer quotations are useful for usage, not proof of ancient etymology.

title: Matalj Bukovski Cuvée — current product descriptions
provenance: Current Serbian retail product record reproducing producer wine composition
summary: Identifies current Negotinska Krajina wine Bukovski Cuvée as Prokupac, Začinak and 7% Četereška, demonstrating live regional wine usage of the name. It does not show Četereška as a standalone front-label variety.
notes: Composition is consistent across multiple current retailers; a producer technical sheet would be preferable for archival certainty.

title: Vinarija Tonković — Kadarka
provenance: Current primary producer narrative and portfolio
summary: Uses Kadarka on current wines and reports that the cultivar appeared as Skadarka in Bolić's 1816 book and the Venčac cooperative, while presenting loss of the initial s and the Skadar derivation as a migration story rather than documented linguistics.
notes: Primary for Tonković naming, interested and promotional for the etymological narrative; the page also misspells Bolić as Belić in one version.

title: SerbianWine.rs — current indigenous-grape overview and Kadarka winery records
summary: The current indigenous-grape overview has no dedicated Kadarka/Skadarka/Četereška terminology section; its Maurer winery record uses Kadarka for current wines but provides no etymology or evidence that all three forms appear on labels.
notes: Only public pages were used; no hidden, blurred or Premium material was accessed.

title: Vranac; Tamjanika; Žametovka
summary: The expanded Vranac article describes intense ruby colour, full body and suitability both for blending and varietal styles; Tamjanika is intensely aromatic; Žametovka/Kavčina is light red and blend-associated. English Wikipedia has no useful Začinak or Župski Bojadiser article and does not establish Serbian mixed-planting history.
notes: Vranac article now cites CANU and peer-reviewed sources; local helper-grape claims still require Serbian institutional evidence.

title: Vranac; Gelber Muskateller; Žametovka — deutschsprachige Wikipedia
provenance: German Wikipedia article cluster and search
summary: Links the Vranac/Vranec name with deep wine colour and describes Muscat aromaticity, but offers no Serbian Začinak, Župski Bojadiser or mixed-vineyard evidence and no support for Kavčina as a bouquet corrector.
notes: German Wikipedia is subordinate to Serbian university and CEVVIN profiles for locally bred cultivars.

title: Sárga muskotály; Vranac; Kavčina — magyar Wikipédia keresés
summary: Provides general Muscat aromatic context but no dedicated Vranac, Začinak, Župski Bojadiser or Serbian field-blend coverage and no evidence for a Kavčina bouquet role.
notes: The absence of local Serbian cultivars is recorded explicitly rather than inferred as contradiction.

title: Вранац; Тамјаника — српска Википедија и претрага
provenance: Serbian Wikipedia article cluster and search
summary: Supports Tamjanika's powerful Muscat aroma and independent wine identity and supplies general Vranac context, but lacks robust dedicated coverage of Začinak and Župski Bojadiser and does not document the mixed-planting thesis or Kavčina bouquet function.
notes: CEVVIN gives materially stronger Serbian viticultural and oenological descriptions.

title: Вранац; Мускат белый — русская Википедия и поиск
provenance: Russian Wikipedia article cluster and search
summary: Confirms broad Vranac and Muscat identity and style context but has no sourced treatment of Serbian Začinak, Župski Bojadiser, Kavčina's proposed bouquet role or the history of Serbian mixed vineyards.
notes: Russian terminology adds no independent local evidence.

title: Vranac; Žametovka; Muškat bijeli — hrvatska Wikipedija i pretraga
provenance: Croatian Wikipedia article cluster and search
summary: Provides regional Vranac and Žametovka/Kavčina context but no reliable evidence for Serbian Začinak, Župski Bojadiser, Tamjanika-neutral-grape practice or a universal mixed-planting design rule.
notes: Croatian regional terminology is relevant to Kavčina identity but not sufficient to assign a bouquet function.

title: CEVVIN — Začinak
provenance: Serbian Center for Viticulture and Winemaking national variety profile
summary: Classifies Začinak among teinturier-type grapes because its must is semi-coloured, describes dark red-black extract-rich wine and states that it is mainly used to improve the colour of other varieties' wines; it records only 0.08 ha of commercial vineyards.
notes: The page also shows a varietal wine is possible, so the role is principal rather than exclusive.

title: University of Belgrade Faculty of Agriculture — Župski bojadiser
summary: Identifies Župski Bojadiser as Alicante Bouschet × Gamay, recognized in 1979, with very coloured juice and extract-rich intensely coloured wine used to correct wines lacking colour.
notes: Strongest source for the created cultivar's intended use.

title: CEVVIN — Župski bojadiser
provenance: Serbian Center for Viticulture and Winemaking national variety profile
summary: Independently confirms intense juice and wine colour and says the cultivar primarily strengthens colour intensity in red wines; the profile ranks it 34th in commercial area and notes very small average parcels.
notes: Only publicly rendered text used; protected-copy controls were not bypassed.

title: CEVVIN — Tamjanika bela
provenance: Serbian Center for Viticulture and Winemaking national variety profile
summary: Describes pronounced Muscat aroma and flavour, ordinary varietal wine, dessert wine and explicit use to improve the taste and smell of wines from other cultivars; it ranks Tamjanika 16th in Serbian commercial plantings.
notes: The profile treats Tamjanika as a group of variants and cautions against oversimplified identity with one Muscat accession.

title: Montenegrin Academy of Sciences and Arts material summarized in Vranac
provenance: English Wikipedia section citing CANU Lexicon of Viticulture and Winemaking of Montenegro (2021)
summary: The cited academy lexicon describes Vranac as intensely ruby, full-bodied, blackberry/blueberry and spice-led, suitable for multiple styles and for blending with other varieties' wines.
notes: The direct CANU interface was not reliably retrievable, so the audit identifies the precise secondary citation pathway rather than pretending direct access.

title: Decanter — World Vranec Day: award-winning wines
provenance: Major international wine publication and current competition results
summary: Characterizes Vranec as typically varietal, deep red and full-bodied with high tannin and acidity; lists both 100% Vranac and Vranac-dominant blend examples.
notes: Competition-oriented, but the general style agrees with academy and peer-reviewed evidence.

title: Vinogradar, vinogradar–rasadničar, podrumar — cultivar use excerpts
summary: Says Začinak's strongly coloured wine corrects other varieties' colour, while Kavčina gives weaker wine associated with Cviček; it supplies no support for Kavčina as a bouquet enhancer.
notes: OCR contains typographic errors; only clear qualitative statements are used.

title: Taste Slovenia — Žametovka / Modra Kavčina
provenance: Slovenian national food and wine presentation
summary: Describes Žametovka/Modra Kavčina as producing high-acid, light-coloured wines that mostly enter simple local blends such as Cviček, Metliška Črnina and red Bizeljčan; it does not call the grape aromatic or bouquet-enhancing.
notes: Relevant if the book means Žametovka by Kavčina; wein.plus notes nomenclatural ambiguity, so identity should be stated explicitly.

title: wein.plus Lexicon — Žametovka; Kavčina Crna
provenance: Publicly visible specialist wine lexicon entries
summary: Lists Kavčina Crna/Modra Kavčina among Žametovka names but a separate Kavčina Crna entry questions exact genetic identity and reports no 2016 plantings; the public text gives no bouquet-correcting function.
notes: Only open text was used; Premium continuation was not accessed or reconstructed.

title: Vinski put Župa — Podrum Mihajlović
summary: Documents a Prokupac wine with a small proportion of Župski Bojadiser and an Italian Riesling–Tamjanika blend described as aromatic and harmonious, directly illustrating colour and aroma helper roles in current Župa practice.
notes: Producer-originated commercial descriptions; used as examples rather than universal proof.

title: Vinum USA — Tenuta Est Stara Ružica and Stara Kupaža
provenance: Current importer technical records for Negotin mixed-vineyard wines
summary: Documents a mixed Negotin vineyard containing Prokupac, Blaufränkisch, Začinak, Vranac, Crna Tamjanika, red and white international cultivars; Stara Ružica is harvested and co-fermented together, while Stara Kupaža explicitly pays homage to the old wine culture of Rogljevo, Smedovac and Rajac.
notes: A modern restoration and commercial interpretation, not proof that every old Serbian vineyard was designed by a fixed recipe.

title: SerbianWine.rs — Tamjanika: Aromatic White Wine and Where to Taste It
summary: Describes Tamjanika as intensely aromatic and commonly made as a dry varietal white, while also noting sparkling, late-harvest and blend interpretations and listing current producers where it can be tasted.
notes: Public editorial page only; no Premium or obscured material used.

title: English Wikipedia — Pamid
summary: Calls Pamid an old red grape associated with Bulgaria and grown in Serbia and neighbouring countries; describes light, low-acid, low-extract wine for young consumption. It does not cover Plovdina/Slankamenka synonymy, CEVVIN rank, Leposavić, VIVC's institutional scope or Drenak homonymy, and the page currently warns that it cites no sources.
notes: The Thracian-age assertion is unsourced on the page and receives less weight than peer-reviewed genetics and institutional data.

title: German Wikipedia — Pamid
summary: Gives VIVC 8899, Bulgaria–Greece border origin, red berries, pale/low-acid young wine and a long synonym list including Crvena Slankamenka, Plovdina and Drenak. It does not recognize the Drenak–Parmak Cerven collision or the Serbian site, rank and group details.
notes: Its synonym list is catalogue-derived and should not be read as proof that each local name uniquely denotes Pamid.

title: Hungarian Wikipedia — Piros szlanka
provenance: Requested Hungarian Wikipedia corpus; interlanguage link and Hungarian Wikibooks index confirm the article title
summary: The Hungarian corpus has an interlanguage article under Piros szlanka, the Hungarian Pamid name, but its article body was not retrievable in this pass. No accessible Hungarian Wikipedia evidence was used for the Serbian rank, Leposavić, sensory detail or Drenak identity conflict.
notes: No factual statement beyond page identity is attributed to an inaccessible body; specialist Hungarian-form evidence is cross-checked through VIVC-derived sources.

title: Serbian Wikipedia search — Pamid / Plovdina / Slankamenka Crvena / Drenak
summary: No dedicated Serbian Wikipedia article or relevant passage was found for Pamid/Plovdina/Slankamenka Crvena or the Drenak identity collision.
notes: Serbian institutional CEVVIN and the peer-reviewed Serbian-vineyard study therefore carry the Serbian-language/content burden.

title: Russian Wikipedia — Памид
summary: Identifies Pamid as VIVC 8899, a Bulgarian-associated red wine grape cultivated in neighbouring countries, and describes light red, low-acid wines without ageing potential. It repeats a Thracian-origin story but gives no Plovdina synonym set, Serbian rank/site or Drenak analysis.
notes: The article is tagged as lacking sources; its historical superlatives are not treated as independent proof.

title: Croatian Wikipedia search — Pamid / Plovdina / Slankamenka Crvena / Drenak
summary: No dedicated Croatian Wikipedia article or relevant passage was found for the cultivar identity, wine style, Serbian planting rank or Drenak homonymy.
notes: Absence in this small corpus is explicit and not treated as negative evidence about the cultivar.

title: CEVVIN — Slankamenka
provenance: Serbian Centre for Viticulture and Oenology cultivar inventory
summary: Lists Slankamenka under «Grupa Plovina» with Slankamenka Crvena, Plovdina colour forms and Drenak; calls it a very old Balkan cultivar; ranks it 22nd in commercial vineyards; and describes harmonious, drinkable, thin, lower-alcohol, neutral/simple wine often showing a slight reddish hue.
notes: The grouping is a Serbian institutional presentation; it does not resolve every genetically distinct accession carried under Drenak.

title: Frontiers in Plant Science 2024 — genetic characterization of old Serbian grapevines
summary: Genotyped 138 old Serbian vines at 7 SSR and 240 SNP loci; identified 29 samples as Pamid, generally prospected as Plovdina or Lisičina, and one as Parmak Cerven. The discussion explicitly maps Drenak to Parmak Cerven and warns that the analyses do not date cultivation history.
notes: The main article does not connect the Pamid samples to Lakićević/Leposavić and does not display the exact field name of the one Parmak Cerven accession; those details require separate primary or supplementary evidence.

title: VIVC passport 8899 — Pamid
provenance: Vitis International Variety Catalogue, Julius Kühn-Institut; passport identity reflected in peer-reviewed Table 1 and catalogue-derived encyclopedia records
summary: Canonical identity anchor for Pamid, VIVC 8899, with the published synonym tradition including Crvena Slankamenka, Plovdina and Drenak.
notes: Direct automated retrieval returned 403; no sensory or historical inference is attributed to the inaccessible passport.

title: Julius Kühn Institute — Information Centre Grapevine and Wine
summary: Defines VIVC as a scientifically curated worldwide grapevine catalogue with about 23,500 varieties, wild species and breeding lines and variety-specific passport, description, photo and bibliography data; related JKI material says genetic fingerprints expose synonyms, homonyms and misnomers.
notes: Corrects the book's colloquial «every name of every vine» wording to cultivar/accession-level curated data.

title: wein.plus Lexicon — Pamid
summary: Public text places the red cultivar in the Bulgaria/Greece border region and maps Serbian Slankamenka Crvena, North Macedonian Plovdina, Hungarian Piros Szlanka and Bulgarian Drenak to Pamid.
notes: Only openly visible text was used; Premium continuation was neither accessed nor reconstructed.

title: wein.plus Lexicon — Parmak Cerven
provenance: User-requested large specialist wine lexicon, public entry
summary: Independently lists Drenak, Drenak Rouge, Strumicki Drenok and Valandovski Drenak among Parmak Cerven names, while the Pamid entry also uses Drenak, directly demonstrating the name collision inside one curated specialist resource.
notes: The entry describes a table-grape identity and is used for nomenclature, not wine tasting descriptors.

title: wein.plus Lexicon — Slankamenka
summary: Treats unqualified Slankamenka as a white Banat cultivar and says a possible genetic relationship to red Pamid/Slankamenka Crvena is unknown, demonstrating why the colour qualifier is essential.
notes: Only open text was used; it reveals a nomenclatural conflict with the broad CEVVIN group rather than resolving it.

title: SerbianWine.rs — Serbian Grape Varieties: Indigenous, Historic and Modern
summary: The current overview covers Prokupac, Tamjanika, Smederevka, Grašac Beli, Bagrina and Morava, but contains no Pamid, Plovdina, Slankamenka Crvena or Drenak section and therefore supplies no confirmation for this block.
notes: Explicit source gap; absence from one overview is not proof of national insignificance.

title: Vinarija Lakićević — History
provenance: Producer account previously captured in this audit as E001691
summary: The winery attributes identification of Pamid/Slankamenka red in old Banjska-area vineyard material to genetic testing, but publishes no laboratory, sample table, markers or report on the page.
notes: A producer-originated claim, not an independent scientific publication; the current page presented an automated-access challenge, so the already captured public text trail is preserved without embellishment.

title: English Wikipedia — Welschriesling
summary: Maps Welschriesling to Riesling Italico, Graševina and Serbian Grašac, distinguishes it from Rhine Riesling, calls it widely planted in Serbia and presents mutually competing Roman, eastern-Balkan and Champagne origin traditions rather than a settled Sremski Karlovci birthplace.
notes: Its Serbian planting superlative reflects older data and is superseded for current rank by the official 2025 Vineyard Register.

title: German Wikipedia — Welschriesling
summary: Confirms the international synonym set and distinctness from Rhine Riesling, identifies Coccalona Nera parentage and favours northern Italian or Champagne origin hypotheses. It gives no support for Sremski Karlovci as the demonstrated birthplace or for the current Serbian white-cultivar rank.
notes: The infobox's Italian origin is more definite than the underlying 2020 genetic paper permits.

title: Hungarian Wikipedia — Olaszrizling
summary: Uses the Hungarian Olaszrizling name for the same cultivar and discusses Italian or French origin traditions. It contains no Serbian acreage, workhorse classification, Sremski Karlovci herbarium argument or evidence of Serbian genetic origin.
notes: Useful for Hungarian nomenclature; not an authority on current Serbian vineyard statistics.

title: Serbian Wikipedia — Грашевина
summary: Defines Graševina/Italian Riesling as a Central European white cultivar distinct from Rhine Riesling. The short page supplies no current Serbian area rank, no formal local/international taxonomy and no Sremski Karlovci origin evidence.
notes: Local-language relevance does not outweigh the official register or peer-reviewed genealogy.

title: Russian Wikipedia — Вельшрислинг
summary: Confirms Welschriesling/Riesling Italico and other regional names, distinguishes the cultivar from Riesling and explicitly treats origin as unclear across northern-Italian, eastern-Balkan and unsupported Champagne hypotheses. Serbian rank and cultural domestication are absent.
notes: Substantially follows the English article and is not counted as a wholly independent origin analysis.

title: Croatian Wikipedia — Graševina
summary: Identifies Graševina with Welschriesling/Italian Riesling and presents it as an important Central European regional cultivar, including a Croatian autochthonous tradition. It does not support a Serbian birthplace or current Serbian acreage rank.
notes: The page's sourcing is weak, so its national-origin tradition is recorded but not privileged.

title: Ministry of Agriculture — Green Book 2025, Book II
provenance: Official Serbian Ministry report based on the Vineyard Register, chart 46
summary: For vineyards intended for commercial grape production at end-2025, chart 46 gives Merlot 12%, Cabernet Sauvignon 10%, Chardonnay 9% and Grašac 8%. Thus Grašac is a major workhorse but no longer the leading white cultivar in this current register snapshot.
notes: The register covers predominantly commercial parcels, not every household, abandoned or unregistered vine in Serbia; chart shares must not be generalized beyond that population.

title: Scientific Reports 2020 — DNA-based genealogy of Welschriesling and northwestern Italian cultivars
summary: Identifies old northwestern-Italian Coccalona Nera as one parent of Riesling Italico/Welschriesling/Graševina, with the other parent unknown; the authors cannot choose between Central Europe and northwestern Italy as the crossing location.
notes: Italian parentage does not by itself prove that the offspring originated in Italy, and the study does not identify Sremski Karlovci.

title: GuildSomm — Grow Welschriesling/Graševina/Grašac
provenance: Current specialist synthesis by Caroline Gilby MW
summary: Explains Grašac/Graševina naming, its widespread Serbian role and modern name revival; records Graschaz in a Sremski Karlovci herbarium dated 1812–1824 but leaves genetic origin open between Central Europe and northwestern Italy.
notes: The herbarium establishes early documented presence, not birthplace.

title: wein.plus Wine Guide — Serbia cultivar area table
provenance: User-requested specialist database; public unobscured regional table
summary: An older public table lists Welschriesling/Graševina at 2,037 ha ahead of Chardonnay at 1,455 ha and among Serbia's largest cultivars, explaining the formerly common «leading white» description.
notes: The table's reference year and methodology differ from the Ministry's end-2025 commercial register; no Premium material was used.

title: wein.plus Lexicon — Welschriesling
summary: Public text presents Welschriesling as an old, widely distributed Danube-basin/Central European cultivar with many country-specific names, illustrating international reach and disputed national ownership.
notes: Only openly visible text was used; the lexicon's Croatia/old-Austria origin formula remains one hypothesis and is not allowed to override peer-reviewed uncertainty.

title: SerbianWine.rs — Serbian Grape Varieties: Indigenous, Historic and Modern
summary: Places Grašac Beli among Serbia's historic regional whites and links it internationally to Welschriesling, supporting cultural domestication without calling it an ancient Serbian autochthon.
notes: The overview gives no acreage or origin proof; SerbianWine.rs winery pages nevertheless show Grašac across multiple current Srem portfolios.

title: VIVC passport 13217 — Welschriesling
provenance: Vitis International Variety Catalogue, Julius Kühn-Institut; identity reflected in requested Wikipedias and scientific literature
summary: Canonical cultivar identity anchor for Welschriesling and its multinational synonym tradition, separate from Rhine Riesling VIVC 10077.

title: English Wikipedia — Gewürztraminer
summary: Defines an aromatic pink-skinned white-wine cultivar, lists Traminac and Traminac Mirisavi among names, gives lychee, rose, passion fruit and floral notes, and explains high natural sugar and acidity-balance difficulty. It also warns that Traminer family names are genetically and commercially unstable.

title: German Wikipedia — Gewürztraminer
summary: Distinguishes Gewürztraminer as an aromatic form within the broader Traminer/Savagnin family and describes strong rose, lychee and spice aromatics with rich, low-acid wine styles. It gives no Fruška Gora ranking.

title: Hungarian Wikipedia — Tramini
summary: Uses Tramini for the Traminer/Gewürztraminer complex and emphasizes intense floral-spicy aroma. Serbian terminology, specific structural claims and Fruška Gora quality ranking are absent.

title: Serbian Wikipedia search — Траминац / Гевирцтраминер
provenance: Requested Serbian Wikipedia corpus search and interlanguage review
summary: No sufficiently detailed retrievable Serbian Wikipedia article was found to verify the cultivar-name boundary, sensory structure, sweetness perception or claim that Fruška Gora has Serbia's best versions.

title: Russian Wikipedia — Гевюрцтраминер
summary: Confirms the aromatic Gewürztraminer/Traminer relationship and typical lychee, rose and spice-led profile. It does not establish Serbian label identity, current Srem examples or regional supremacy.

title: Croatian Wikipedia — Traminac
summary: Shows that Traminac is also Croatian regional usage and associates the family with strongly aromatic wine. It does not reliably separate every Traminer form or compare Serbian regions.

title: wein.plus Lexicon — Gewürztraminer

title: Decanter — Gewürztraminer grape profile

title: Vin de France — Gewurztraminer grape profile
summary: Describes Gewürztraminer as moderately/low acid, strong, rich, smooth and very full-bodied, with lychee, grapefruit and dried apricot, and capable of dry through sweet styles.

title: Food & Wine — Gewürztraminer guide
provenance: Major food and wine publication synthesis
summary: Gives ginger and lemongrass among spice notes, describes relatively full body and low acidity, and directly explains that the fruit can seem sweeter even when the wine is dry.

title: SerbianWine.rs corpus search — Traminac / Fruška Gora

provenance: Independent professional tastings by Peter Moser, 2022–2023

notes: Several wines from one regional tasting program demonstrate quality but do not rank Fruška Gora against every Serbian Traminac region or vintage.

title: English Wikipedia — Vranac
provenance: Highest-priority requested Wikipedia; current expanded article with academy and peer-reviewed references
summary: Current article identifies Montenegrin origin and Kratošija × Duljenga parentage, documents Serbian cultivation, and gives the strongest sourced consensus as full body, intense ruby colour, blackberry, blueberry and dried spice. Older cached wording contained the exact young-purple, jam, one-to-two-year and mature-aroma formula, but that wording is not treated as independent evidence; the current page does not verify the name etymology.
notes: The current wine-characteristics paragraph cites CANU. Exact maturation chronology found in older versions is compared separately with the still-current Croatian text.

title: German Wikipedia — Vranac
summary: Defines Vranac as a Balkan red cultivar grown in Montenegro, Serbia, North Macedonia and southern Croatia and glosses Vranec as «black stallion», connecting the name to deep wine colour. It provides no fruit or mature-aroma profile, acidity, service or current pedigree.
notes: Its origin and synonym section is dated and substantially less informative than current EN/SR and CANU material.

title: Hungarian Wikipedia search — Vranac / Vranec
provenance: Requested Hungarian Wikipedia corpus and interlanguage-link review
summary: No dedicated Hungarian Wikipedia article or useful Hungarian material was found for Vranac identity, etymology, descriptors, ageing, serving or decanting.

title: Serbian Wikipedia — Вранац (грожђе)
provenance: Requested local-language encyclopedia; expanded article citing CANU and peer-reviewed research
summary: Confirms Montenegrin origin, Kratošija × Duljenga parentage, Serbian cultivation, full body, intense ruby colour, blackberry, blueberry and dried spice, and explains that phenolics affect colour, astringency and ageing potential. It does not give the name etymology, the book's exact service or one-to-two-year chronology.
notes: Closely parallels current English article and shares CANU sources; agreement is not counted as fully independent.

title: Russian Wikipedia — Вранац
summary: Directly states that Serbian «вранац» is cognate with Russian «вороной» and means a black-coated horse; gives Balkan distribution and a dark-ruby, more-complex bouquet after one to two years, but no detailed descriptor, acidity, oak, temperature or decanting evidence.
notes: The etymology is independently checked against Vasmer and a South Slavic dictionary; the wine paragraph is too lightly sourced to establish a universal timetable.

title: Croatian Wikipedia — Vranac (vino)
provenance: Requested Croatian-language encyclopedia; short unsourced article
summary: Contains almost the book's complete formula: bright-purple young wine with fruit jam, strong tannins and medium-high acidity; after one or two years dark ruby with cinnamon, chocolate, liquorice, flowers, dark fruit, herbs and oak; claims oak/bottle ageing is often necessary and advises room-temperature service.
notes: The page has no references and appears in the same translation/reuse family as older English descriptions; lexical agreement must not be mistaken for independent corroboration.

title: Montenegrin Academy of Sciences and Arts — Leksikon vinogradarstva i vinarstva Crne Gore: Vranac
provenance: Authoritative national-academy cultivar entry by Vesna Maraš
summary: Documents Crmnica origin, Kratošija × Duljenga parentage, spread to central Serbia, full body, intense ruby colour, blackberry, blueberry, dried spice, 12–14% alcohol and about 5–6 g/L wine acidity, plus multiple styles and blending potential.
notes: Does not prescribe an exact one-to-two-year transformation, mandatory oak, 18°C or decanting; a displayed must-acidity range appears typographically corrupt and is not used.

title: Vasmer Etymological Dictionary — вороной / ворон
provenance: Russian edition of Max Vasmer's etymological dictionary
summary: Connects Russian вороной with Macedonian/Bulgarian вран, Serbo-Croatian vran and other Slavic cognates, deriving the colour word from ворон.
notes: Checks the book's Russian comparison linguistically rather than relying on wine marketing.

title: Hrvatski jezični portal — vranac
summary: Defines vranac as a horse of vran, black coat and directs the etymology to vran.
notes: The ordinary noun means a black horse; «stallion» is a common wine-language intensification, not the only literal gloss.

title: BKWine/Forbes — Vranec/Vranac grape profile
provenance: Independent specialist journalist profile by Per Karlsson
summary: Reports near-opaque dark colour, blackberry, blueberry, plum, cherry/cassis, spice, herbs and chocolate; notes that oak-aged examples can show vanilla/toffee and that tannin and acidity are usually prominent but tannins may be soft.
notes: Useful counterweight to the copied encyclopedia formula because it explicitly cautions against overgeneralizing tannin from colour.

title: Vranec World Day / Wines of Macedonia — About Vranec
provenance: Regional promotional organisation backed by Wines of Macedonia
summary: Gives 6–7 g/L grape acidity, deep purple colour, black ripe fruit, full body and tannin; separately repeats young bright-purple strawberry-jam/forest-fruit and aged dark-ruby chocolate/cinnamon/black-fruit/herb/oak profiles.
notes: Supports the tradition behind the book wording, not a universal one-to-two-year transition or an independent scientific consensus.

title: Raičević et al. — Polyphenolic content and sensory profile of Montenegrin Vranac
provenance: Peer-reviewed Macedonian Journal of Chemistry and Chemical Engineering, DOI 10.20450/mjcce.2017.1145
summary: Shows experimentally that vintage, maceration system, enzyme, oak chips and added grape tannin change Vranac phenolics, colour and sensory profile.
notes: The abstract supports process dependence; it does not validate every named aroma or mandate oak ageing.

title: Bordeaux.com — How to serve wine
summary: Recommends 16–18°C for structured or ageworthy reds and a first-nose/second-nose test before decanting; young wines generally tolerate air better than old fragile bottles.

provenance: 2026 peer-reviewed study using VIVC origin and pedigree data
summary: Classifies Morava as a Serbian white interspecific hybrid and gives ((Kunbarat × Tramin) × Bianca) × Rajnai Rizling GM 239-20; Table 3 explicitly records no crossing-year data.

summary: Gives breeder, Karlovci, full pedigree and 2003 approval; reports vigorous vines, variable yield, high acidity, high grey-mould/downy-mildew resistance, non-omissible powdery-mildew protection, good frost tolerance and elegant fresh Sauvignon-like wine.

title: Croatian Wikipedia search — Serbian autochthonous-grape conservation
provenance: Requested Croatian Wikipedia corpus and searches for Serbian local cultivars, clearing and genetic resources

notes: Croatian material about individual regional cultivars is not a substitute for Serbian conservation-program evidence.

title: CEVVIN — Autohtone i regionalne sorte vinove loze Srbije
provenance: Primary 2019 institutional catalogue by Serbia's Centre for Viticulture and Winemaking
summary: Page 1 calls mass grubbing-up and deterioration of local-variety vineyards in a previous period a basic problem, says special programmes had not saved those vineyards and selected the best material before clearing, and describes the lost areas as a permanent loss of grapevine genetic potential; it then presents an active CEVVIN programme.
notes: The source says 'previous period' rather than a dated set of decades and does not call clearing the single cause of all present-day scarcity.

title: CEVVIN — Genetički resursi
provenance: Current official genetic-resources page of Serbia's Centre for Viticulture and Winemaking
summary: Says old traditional-variety vineyards disappear through abandonment and economically motivated clearing; calls each unexamined and cleared local-variety vineyard irreplaceable, then details inventory, field evaluation, GIS, databases, propagation, collection-vineyard preservation and clonal selection.
notes: The simultaneous loss and conservation activity contradicts a simple all-or-nothing account of unprotected chance survival.

title: Jakšić et al. — Classification of Sustainability Potential of Genetic Resources of Local Grapevine Varieties in Serbia
provenance: 2024 original article in Matica Srpska Journal of Natural Sciences, DOI 10.2298/ZMSPN2446091J
summary: Reports 31 local wine varieties among 224 commercial grapevine varieties, repeats the mass-grubbing, deterioration, missing special-programme and permanent-loss account, but also models 10,402 local-variety vineyards, separates endangered from sustainable holdings and notes that some local cultivars are expanding while others approach disappearance.
notes: The paper supports the institutional loss diagnosis but not a claim that every local cultivar survives only by chance or that none was preserved.

title: Tello et al. — The genetic characterization of grapevines prospected in old Serbian vineyards
provenance: 2024 original research article in Frontiers in Plant Science
summary: Documents older phylloxera losses and replacement with foreign cultivars, then analyses 138 vines from extant old Serbian vineyards; the sample also includes some isolated vines that survived clearing in meadows and forest edges, revealing both deliberate prospection and a limited chance-survivor pathway.
notes: The study says Serbia preserves a high number of local varieties and does not generalize isolated survivors to the entire present assortment.

title: Sivčev, Ranković-Vasić and Radovanović — Clone selection in old vineyards of southeastern and eastern Serbia
provenance: 2011 original research article in Genetika, DOI 10.2298/GENSR1103465S
summary: Reports that clone and sanitary selection to preserve old-vineyard varieties began in southeastern Serbia in 2006, examined 1,048 vines and selected candidates including Prokupac; work expanded to eastern Serbia in 2008.
notes: This does not disprove CEVVIN's claim that many vineyards were lost without prior programmes, but it rules out reading 'programmes did not exist' as an unlimited statement about all recent Serbian work.

title: Pržić and Marković — Clonal selection and valorisation of autochthonous grape cultivars in Serbia
summary: Calls Serbia's autochthonous assortment reduced to a few cultivars and reports first varietal-selection results for Smederevka and Prokupac, with four and twelve selected clones respectively.
notes: The narrow first-selection statement concerns these two cultivars and cannot establish that no earlier preservation project existed for any Serbian grape.

title: English Wikipedia — Kadarka, Prokupac, Tamjanika, Vranac and Serbian wine
provenance: Requested English Wikipedia corpus and linked cultivar searches
summary: Presents Prokupac as Serbian, Vranac as Montenegrin, white Tamjanika as belonging to the Muscat family and Kadarka origin as disputed between a Shkodër-area and Hungarian hypothesis; it neither documents the CEVVIN publication's exact status nor Petrović's full position, Bagrina classification or the methodological limits of the 2024 Serbian genetic study.

title: German Wikipedia — Weinbau in Serbien
provenance: Requested German Wikipedia corpus and linked Prokupac and Vranac articles
summary: Groups Prokupac, Kadarka, Tamjanika, Smederevka, Vranac and Krstač as regional Serbian-wine cultivars; the linked Prokupac article calls that cultivar Serbian and the linked Vranac article gives a wider southern-Yugoslav distribution, but the corpus does not reproduce CEVVIN's internal status distinctions or Petrović's claims.

title: Hungarian Wikipedia — Kadarka
summary: States that Kadarka's origin is uncertain, with Asia Minor and Albania proposed, and that it reached Hungary from the Balkans, probably through Serbian mediation, in the eighteenth century; it provides no evidence for the other cultivars, CEVVIN source status or Petrović attribution.

title: Serbian Wikipedia — Прокупац and linked cultivar searches

notes: The Serbian Tamjanika infobox is weaker than the primary genetic and VIVC evidence and is recorded as a corpus result, not adopted as consensus.

title: Russian Wikipedia — Виноделие в Сербии and Кадарка
provenance: Requested Russian Wikipedia corpus and linked cultivar search
summary: Lists Prokupac, Vranac, Tamjanika and Kadarka among Serbian-grown cultivars and calls Tamjanika a local mutation of white Muscat; the separate Kadarka page records broad Balkan and Hungarian distribution but no origin analysis. The corpus does not support the exact professor attribution or the claimed French derivation.
notes: The unsourced mutation wording is not sufficient to override CEVVIN's non-prejudgment or the 2024 genetic identification of sampled Tamjanika Ćilibarka as Muscat à Petits Grains.

title: Croatian Wikipedia — Kadarka and Vranac

notes: The Croatian pages demonstrate the instability of national-origin labels rather than establishing a single origin centre.

title: CEVVIN — Autohtone i regionalne sorte vinove loze Srbije
provenance: Primary 2019 institutional publication by Serbia's Centre for Viticulture and Winemaking
summary: Its commercial-vineyard list combines autochthonous and regional cultivars. It calls Tamjanika crna regional and international, Kavčina Central European and grown in Austria and Germany, Vranac a cultivar of Montenegro, and Prokupac the most important Serbian autochthonous cultivar; for the white Tamjanika group it explicitly avoids prejudging origin.
notes: This expert publication is not the statutory Serbian variety register; its mixed umbrella is central to interpreting the word 'local'.

title: CEVVIN — O Centru
summary: States that the Republic of Serbia founded CEVVIN, that it is a national expert and research institution, and that it performs vineyard-register and other professional work for ministries.
notes: Institutional authority does not turn every CEVVIN publication into a statutory register or legal classification instrument.

title: Danas — Vinska mapa Srbije: Profesor Aleksandar Petrović otkriva gde nastaju najbolji rizlinzi, šardonei i prokupci
provenance: 9 April 2025 interview reproduced from vinologija.rs; identifies Petrović as an associate professor at the University of Belgrade Faculty of Agriculture
summary: Petrović calls Prokupac the only certain Serbian original cultivar but immediately allows Začinak and possibly Kreaca; says Bagrina is considered Romanian; treats black Tamjanika as uncertain and identifies white Tamjanika with Muscat Blanc à Petits Grains and its Frontignan and Austrian names while leaving origin uncertain. Kadarka is not discussed.
notes: The article supports reporting his view, not promoting every view to genetic or catalogue consensus; Muscat de Frontignan is presented as an alternative name, not a French ancestor.

title: NIN — Gde je Srbija na vinskoj karti Evrope
summary: Quotes Petrović treating Kadarka as a name derived from Skadarka while noting a Hungarian claim, and later calls Začinak almost certainly Serbia's second autochthonous cultivar after Prokupac.
notes: The Kadarka passage does not itself say Montenegro; that geography enters through the separate Lake Skadar origin hypothesis.

title: VIVC passport — KADARKA KEK
provenance: Scientifically curated Vitis International Variety Catalogue passport
summary: Assigns KADARKA KEK VIVC 5898 to Hungary and records its international identity and synonyms.
notes: A catalogue country assignment is relevant evidence but does not by itself settle competing historical birthplace and transmission hypotheses.

title: VIVC passport — BRAGHINA ROSIE
provenance: Scientifically curated Vitis International Variety Catalogue passport
summary: Uses BRAGHINA ROSIE as the prime name for VIVC 1644 and assigns the cultivar to Serbia.
notes: This conflicts with the expert interview's Romanian attribution and requires the book to label that statement as Petrović's view rather than an uncontested fact.

title: VIVC passport — MUSCAT A PETITS GRAINS BLANCS
provenance: Scientifically curated Vitis International Variety Catalogue passport
summary: Records MUSCAT A PETITS GRAINS BLANCS as VIVC 8193 and assigns its country or region of origin to Greece.
notes: The French place-name synonym Frontignan cannot be converted into a French origin or parentage claim without separate evidence.

title: VIVC passport — PROKUPAC
provenance: Scientifically curated Vitis International Variety Catalogue passport
summary: Records PROKUPAC as VIVC 9734 with Serbia as country or region of origin.
notes: This supports Prokupac's Serbian status but does not prove that it is the only Serbian autochthonous cultivar.

title: Tello et al. — The genetic characterization of grapevines prospected in old Serbian vineyards reveals multiple relationships between traditional varieties of the Balkans
provenance: 2024 original research in Frontiers in Plant Science, DOI 10.3389/fpls.2024.1391679
summary: Profiles 138 vines and finds 59 genetic profiles, most in a complex cross-border Balkan pedigree network. It treats Prokupac, Začinak and Braghina Rosie as Serbian in its VIVC-derived table, identifies sampled Tamjanika Ćilibarka as Muscat à Petits Grains, and expressly states that the analyses were not designed to determine cultivation duration in Serbia.
notes: The study can support pedigree and long regional presence in some cases, but it cautions against deriving an exact cultivation timeline; its network does not alone locate a unique birthplace for every cultivar.

title: Jakšić et al. — Classification of Sustainability Potential of Local Grapevine Variety Vineyards in Serbia
provenance: 2024 original research in Matica Srpska Journal for Natural Sciences, DOI 10.2298/ZMSPN2446091J
summary: Explicitly avoids literal name-and-origin taxonomy and defines 'local grapevine varieties' for the paper as autochthonous, regional and old cultivars grown in Serbia for a long time, then lists 31 such wine cultivars.
notes: The definition is a transparent research convention; it does not establish a centuries-long Serbian history or local breeding origin for each listed cultivar.

title: PlantGrape — Kadarka
provenance: French official grape-cultivar catalogue maintained from INRAE and Institut Agro Montpellier resources
summary: Describes Kadarka as originally cultivated in Hungary and the Balkans and possibly of Ottoman origin, and separately records its regulatory names and registrations in European catalogues.
notes: This wider formulation supports caution toward a unique Montenegro-or-Hungary birthplace and separates traditional cultivation area from regulatory registration.

title: English Wikipedia — Serbian wine
summary: Describes Yugoslavia's production peak in the 1970s, quantity-oriented socialism and mass production in large combines such as Navip and Rubin, and lists both international and local cultivars; it gives neither the current 224-cultivar count nor planted-area proof of Western European dominance or supplier-variety control.
notes: The article's current vineyard-area figure is obsolete and was not used; its historical paragraph is treated as secondary context, not as proof of the full causal chain.

title: German Wikipedia — Weinbau in Serbien
summary: Names regional cultivars and international partners such as Riesling, Pinot noir, Gamay, Merlot and Cabernet Sauvignon, but supplies no current cultivar count or area shares and does not cover the socialist combine history, supplier relations or the proposed 1970s causation.
notes: The article's broad regional-versus-international grouping cannot establish comparative planted-area dominance.

title: Hungarian Wikipedia search — Serbian cultivar structure and socialist wine combines
summary: No Hungarian Wikipedia article was found that reports Serbia's current cultivar count or planted-area structure, reconstructs the role of Serbian wine combines in the 1970s or documents control of supplier cultivar choices.
notes: The Szerém wine-region and Kadarka articles provide separate regional history but not evidence for this national Serbian paragraph.

title: Serbian Wikipedia — Виноградарство у Србији
summary: Provides a long unranked list of Serbian-grown cultivars including Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Chardonnay and numerous local varieties; its history ends with early twentieth-century developments and does not quantify current dominance or examine socialist combines and their suppliers.
notes: An unranked list proves cultivation only, not dominance by cultivar origin, count or area.

title: Russian Wikipedia — Виноделие в Сербии
summary: Lists international and local cultivars grown in Serbia but supplies no total cultivar count, planted-area shares or 1970s combine history and no evidence that wineries prescribed suppliers' varieties.
notes: The page was last edited in 2022 and its list is not a statistical distribution.

title: Croatian Wikipedia search — Serbian cultivar structure and Yugoslav wine combines
summary: No Croatian Wikipedia material was found that reports Serbia's cultivar total or area structure or establishes the paragraph's causal sequence from 1970s combines to suppliers' cultivar choices.
notes: General Croatian wine and cultivar pages do not substitute for Serbian national statistics or combine records.

title: Jakšić et al. — Classification of Sustainability Potential of Local Grapevine Variety Vineyards in Serbia
provenance: 2024 original research in Matica Srpska Journal for Natural Sciences, DOI 10.2298/ZMSPN2446091J
summary: Reports 224 cultivars currently used for commercial grape and wine production in Serbia, of which 31 wine cultivars, or 13.84%, are grouped as local; it defines local as an umbrella for autochthonous, regional and long-grown old cultivars.
notes: The share is a share of cultivar names, not planted hectares, and cannot alone prove international area dominance or the relative interest of the groups.

title: CEVVIN — Анализа сектора производње и прераде грожђа и производње вина
provenance: Primary institutional sector study dated 31 March 2019, based on Serbian statistical, vineyard, winery and planting-material registers
summary: Identifies Graševina, Merlot, Cabernet Sauvignon, Chardonnay and Riesling as the five leading international cultivars by registered area, while explicitly treating Graševina as regional but grouping it internationally for that analysis; it also finds recent nursery production dominated by international cultivars and notes the decline of former large social wineries.
notes: Its area data are dated 2019 and its analytical origin categories differ from the 2024 paper's broad local umbrella, so dates, register scope and category rules must be stated.

title: New Europe Wine Guide — Serbia 2026
provenance: 2026 specialist wine guide citing the 2024 Serbian Vineyard Register
summary: Lists the 2024 register's main varieties as Grašac 11%, Chardonnay 9%, Riesling 6%, Sauvignon Blanc 5%, Merlot 11%, Cabernet Sauvignon 9% and Prokupac 5%; the five named international cultivars sum to 40% of total plantings.
