notes: The guide does not reproduce the complete register table, so the listed leaders corroborate importance but are not by themselves a full origin-group total.

title: Marković and Pržić — Serbian Viticulture from the 19th Century to the Present Day
provenance: 2022 historical review in Annals of the University of Craiova, Agriculture, Montanology, Cadastre Series 52/1
summary: Dates intensive vineyard planting to 1959-1970, links it to mechanization and new cultivars, documents large state wineries and intensive plantings of Pinot, Cabernet, Merlot, Riesling, Sauvignon and other cultivars, and gives the land split around 1970 as 106,000 ha individual versus 10,500 ha state sector.
notes: It supports strong state influence and international planting but not the claim that state wineries dictated the varieties planted by private suppliers.

title: Netherlands agricultural network — The vineyard of the Balkans: Wine in Serbia
provenance: 2020 briefing on the Dutch Ministry of Agriculture international network, drawing on Serbian official statistics and registers
summary: Describes large collectivized state-owned companies after the world wars, Yugoslavia's 1970s production peak and the later practice of large wineries buying grapes from small producers; it separately records the continuing category of growers who sell grapes to wine companies.
notes: It does not say those companies prescribed supplier cultivars, and its 135,000 ha figure is the national vineyard total in 1955 rather than a demonstrated company-owned total.

title: Jancis Robinson — Made in Serbia
provenance: 2017 specialist field report by Caroline Gilby MW
summary: Reports that state cooperatives replaced much Prokupac with international cultivars after it was judged unsuitable by the 1960s, describes former state-winery giants and documents the then leading registered variety shares and successful international-cultivar wines.
notes: This moves part of the causal chronology earlier than the book's 1970s formulation and does not quantify who selected varieties in supplier-owned vineyards.

title: Association of Winemakers and Winegrowers of Serbia — I'm picking grapes, I'm choosing tamjanika
provenance: National producer-association page using Serbian Vineyard Register data
summary: States that Serbian grape and wine production is mainly focused on international cultivars and that indigenous, local and newly created cultivars account for about 8% within its cited 5,763.43 ha analysed register scope; it frames local cultivars as carriers of authenticity and local character.
notes: The page gives no publication date and uses a narrower category and register subset than the 2024 local-cultivar paper; its regional-character language remains advocacy, not an objective comparison of interest.

title: Osservatorio Balcani Caucaso Transeuropa — Yugoslav wine: a story of crisis and renovation
provenance: 10 August 2026 historical feature based on sector interviews and OIV and Oxford Companion context
summary: Describes centralized, quota-oriented Yugoslav industrial plants buying grapes from individual growers and the production peak of the 1970s, but does not state that Serbian combines selected or prescribed the suppliers' cultivars.
notes: The feature concerns Yugoslavia broadly and cannot by itself establish a Serbia-specific supplier-planting rule.

title: English Wikipedia — Welschriesling
summary: Maps Welschriesling to Grašac, Graševina, Riesling Italico and Italian Riesling, explicitly distinguishes it from Rhine Riesling and describes wide Central and Southeastern European distribution. It gives no current regional share, revival chronology, Serbian analytical range or detailed sensory profile.
notes: Its claim that the cultivar is Serbia's most planted by total area relies on older data and is not used against the end-2025 commercial register.

title: German Wikipedia — Welschriesling
summary: Confirms synonymy and no relationship to Rhine Riesling; for young dry wine it gives pale green-yellow colour, light structure, floral-fruity aroma dominated by green apple and a brisk fresh palate, while also documenting sweet and sparkling styles. It does not establish Serbian regional shares, revival or analytical ranges.
notes: The generic Austrian-centred profile is useful for style boundaries but cannot be treated as a representative tasting of Serbian Grašac.

title: Hungarian Wikipedia — Olaszrizling
summary: Uses Olaszrizling for the same widely grown Central European cultivar and supplies Hungarian history and general wine context, but no Serbia-specific regional proportion, revival evidence, product chemistry or source-based almond distinction.
notes: Hungarian material helps establish international distribution and nomenclature, not current Serbian denominators.

title: Serbian Wikipedia — Грашевина
summary: Identifies Graševina/Italian Riesling as a Central European white cultivar and distinguishes it from Rhine Riesling. The short page does not substantiate the two regional majority claim, modern revival, exact sensory wording or alcohol and acidity ranges.
notes: Local language does not compensate for absent dates, denominators and product-level evidence.

title: Russian Wikipedia — Вельшрислинг
summary: Confirms the multinational synonym set, uncertain origin and distinction from Rhine Riesling, with general cultivation and wine-style context. It provides no current Serbian regional-share evidence, revival chronology or analytical specification.
notes: The article substantially follows shared international material and is not counted as an independent Serbian statistical line.

title: Croatian Wikipedia — Graševina
summary: Identifies Graševina with Welschriesling/Italian Riesling and describes a usually dry, fresh, slightly bitter regional wine whose aroma varies with site. It does not prove Serbia's two regional majorities, current revival, precise alcohol or acidity range, or the assertion that almond wording lacks sources.
notes: The page has weak legacy sourcing and is used cautiously for the neighbouring regional tradition rather than Serbian statistics.

title: GuildSomm — GROW: A Grape with an Identity Crisis
provenance: Current specialist synthesis by Caroline Gilby MW drawing on genetic and aroma research and regional reporting
summary: Documents the Grašac name revival and Serbia's quality-producer movement, distinguishes the cultivar from Rhine Riesling, and describes light fruity wines with lemon, grapefruit, green apple, white flowers and slight almond bitterness. It stresses wide style variation and says the cultivar was formerly considered neutral and ordinary.
notes: Its Serbian area estimate uses older 13% register data and is not used for the current regional or national rank.

title: Polyphenolic profile, antioxidant and neuroprotective potency of grape juices and wines from Fruška Gora region
provenance: 2017 peer-reviewed article in International Journal of Food Properties
summary: States in its background that Italian Riesling occupied more than half of Fruška Gora vineyards and identifies its Graševina/Olaszrizling synonyms.
notes: The share comes from earlier regional literature rather than the authors' own vineyard inventory; no current official regional breakdown was found.

title: Vinski Vodič — Vršački vinogradi
summary: Reports Italian Riesling at more than 50% of the assortment of Vršački vinogradi, the large enterprise, but does not give the cultivar's share of every vineyard parcel in the wider Vršac wine district.
notes: The company assortment cannot be generalized to the whole region without a dated vineyard-register table.

title: The Buyer — How Central Europe's Grašac white wine variety has been reborn
provenance: 21 November 2025 specialist feature by Ian Bancroft with named Serbian and regional wine professionals
summary: Directly documents the Serbian return to the Grašac name, increased sales, new plot selection and stainless, lees, acacia, barrel, sparkling, sweet and orange experimentation. It gives delicate green-apple, pear and citrus aromas and treats the process as reputational and stylistic revival.
notes: Several causal details are interview testimony and do not constitute a controlled market study; they nevertheless define what the reported revival means.

title: SerbianWine.rs — Grašac Beli: The Serbian White Grape Guide
provenance: User-requested current Serbian public wine guide with cited genetics and tourism sources
summary: Calls Grašac the historic Serbian name of internationally distributed Welschriesling, not a uniquely Serbian genotype, and locates its modern identity on Fruška Gora. Typical dry examples show green or yellow apple, pear, citrus, herbs, hay and a gently bitter finish, while the guide stresses versatility rather than one dramatic aroma.
notes: The page is recent secondary guidance and does not supply a representative chemical dataset or a source for the exact collective oenologist quotation.

title: Erdevik Winery — Geronimo Grašac 2021
summary: Lists a dry 100% Graschatz from Fruška Gora at 12.5% alcohol, 6.14 g/L total acid, 1.80 g/L residual sugar and pH 3.27, with lime, orange peel, Golden Delicious, herbs and a citrus finish.
notes: One vintage supports the common range but cannot define the entire cultivar.

title: Vinarija Verkat — Grašac Beli 2023
provenance: Official winery technical and sensory specification
summary: Gives light yellow-green colour, citrus with dried-herb and green notes, 13% alcohol, 0.5 g/L residual sugar, 6.5 g/L acids and pH 3.15 for a current dry stainless-steel Grašac.
notes: The product fits the book's numerical range but its aromatic profile is not dominated by green apple.

title: Imperator — Cargraš 2024
summary: Lists dry 100% Grašac at 13.5% alcohol, 1.0 g/L residual sugar, pH 3.35 and 5.4 g/L total acidity.
notes: Shows why 11–13% cannot serve as a complete current varietal range even though 5–7 g/L fits this wine.

title: Vino.rs — Vinum grašac horizontally and vertically
provenance: Independent specialist report of a multi-vintage, multi-style Vinum tasting with winemaker data
summary: Records gold-to-green colour, peach, apple and grapefruit in still Grašac, Dina sparkling at just under 12% alcohol and 7.2 g/L acidity, and barrel-aged Grašac 26A 2020 at 14.5% alcohol and 5.8 g/L acidity.
notes: The report demonstrates diversity within one producer; the chemistry is named-wine evidence rather than a population distribution.

title: Vina Srbije — Verkat Grašac Beli 4.0 2021
provenance: Serbian product catalogue reproducing a named wine's technical specification
summary: Lists 13% alcohol, 7.5 g/L acidity and pH 3.10, with citrus, banana, dry herbs and nut notes for a selected low-yield Grašac.
notes: Secondary product data should be checked against the producer if used in the book; it is sufficient here to show that 7 g/L is not a hard upper limit.

title: Serbian wine-product regulation — total acidity expressed as tartaric acid
provenance: Consolidated text of Serbian Official Gazette provisions 26/2015, 93/2015, 41/2017 and 84/2018
summary: Uses the legal analytical formulation 'total acidity, expressed as tartaric acid' in grams per litre, confirming that the book's stated reference acid and unit follow Serbian convention.
notes: The regulation establishes the reporting convention and minima, not a Grašac-specific 5–7 g/L range.

title: Uncorking the Wine World — Vojvodina Wine Show 2019
provenance: Independent 2019 field report by wine writer and international competition judge Ivana Simjanovska
summary: Reports a vertical tasting of Fruškogorski Vinogradi Grašac 2017, 2015 and 2012; the 2012 wine showed marzipan and almond aromas plus marzipan flavour on the palate.
notes: This is a tasting note for one aged wine, not proof that every young Grašac has almond bitterness; it directly disproves the claim that sources only use generic bitterness.

title: Ministry of Agriculture — Green Book 2025, Book II
provenance: Official Serbian Ministry report based on the Vineyard Register, chart 46
summary: At end-2025 Chardonnay accounts for 9% of vineyards intended predominantly for commercial grape production, ranking third overall after Merlot and Cabernet Sauvignon and first among white cultivars.
notes: The register scope does not include every household, abandoned or unregistered vine, and national rank does not make the word «everywhere» literal.

title: Decanter — Explore the Serbia wine region
provenance: Caroline Gilby MW guide produced with Serbian tourism and wine-sector partners
summary: Calls international grapes important to Serbia's transformed modern wine scene and says Chardonnay, Sauvignon Blanc, Cabernet Sauvignon and Merlot do particularly well, citing multiple DWWA Gold and Platinum results; it treats both Vojvodina and central Serbia as major zones.
notes: The page is sponsored and qualitative; the Ministry register supplies the independent quantitative control.

title: DWWA 2026 wine search — Serbia
provenance: Official Decanter World Wine Awards results database
summary: The Serbia result set contains seven 95-point Gold wines. Three are Chardonnay wines: Tarpoš Chardonnay Extra Brut 2021, Zvonko Bogdan Chardonnay 2022 and Zvonko Bogdan Éclater Blanc de Blancs Brut Nature 2018.
notes: The dynamic interface is the primary award index; exact composition of Éclater is confirmed separately by its producer.

title: Tanjug — Srpska vina osvojila tri platinaste medalje na DWWA 2026
provenance: Tanjug report reproducing the Serbian Chamber of Commerce announcement, 19 June 2026
summary: Reports seven Serbian Golds and lists all seven, including the three Chardonnay wines, and separately identifies Deurić La Rem Chardonnay 2023 among three Serbian Platinum wines with 97 points.
notes: The Gold list exactly matches specialist reporting and the official searchable results; the Platinum identity also matches Decanter's official article.

title: Zvonko Bogdan Winery — Eclater 2018
summary: Identifies Éclater harvest 2018 as Chardonnay made by the traditional bottle-fermentation method, with 46 months on lees and zero dosage.
notes: This resolves the otherwise non-obvious cultivar behind the Blanc de Blancs label; the current page intermittently returns a gateway error but remains indexed.

title: Decanter — DWWA 2026 Platinum winners
provenance: Official Decanter World Wine Awards results article
summary: The full Serbia section lists Deurić, La Rem Chardonnay, Fruška Gora, Srem 2023 among the 2026 Platinum winners; the article explains that Platinum wines are retasted Gold winners and occupy the 97-point tier.
notes: The result belongs to the named wine and vintage, not to all Deurić Chardonnay or the cultivar as a whole.

title: New Europe Wine Guide — Serbia 2026
provenance: Beth Willard's current multi-region tasting guide covering 268 named wines from 62 producers over three days in December 2025
summary: Documents Chardonnay across Vojvodina and central Serbia. Northern examples range from elegant, saline La Rem and bright-acid Rajić to full 14.5% Grumen and broad creamy Picus; Šumadija ranges from bright 12% Trijumf sparkling and precise Camille 2024 to opulent Aberdar and very ripe 14.5% Savić 2022.
notes: The guide does not state that the tasting was blind and is not a controlled regional experiment; style and ripeness also reflect vintage, harvest decisions, oak, lees and malolactic choices.

title: English Wikipedia — Chardonnay
summary: Describes Chardonnay as globally planted and highly malleable, with styles shaped by climate, terroir, oak and malolactic fermentation; cooler conditions often give lighter, higher-acid apple and pear profiles, while warmer conditions shift toward peach, melon and tropical fruit.
notes: The article provides the conceptual climate-style model but no Serbian 2026 award list or north-versus-Šumadija comparative sample.

title: German Wikipedia — Chardonnay
summary: Treats Chardonnay as a globally important cultivar capable of very different wines depending on climate and terroir, while also emphasizing ripeness, body and the major influence of oak maturation.
notes: It contains no Serbia-specific 2026 awards or north-central sensory comparison.

title: Hungarian Wikipedia — Chardonnay (szőlőfajta)
summary: Identifies Chardonnay as a worldwide cultivar grown in wine-producing countries across the world.
notes: No Serbian area share, DWWA award arithmetic or regional style comparison is present.

title: Serbian Wikipedia — Шардоне
summary: Defines Chardonnay as a highly sought-after white cultivar of Burgundian origin, now grown worldwide, adaptable to different soils and associated generally with apple, melon and pineapple.
notes: The page does not quantify Serbian plantings, record DWWA 2026 results or distinguish northern and Šumadija wines.

title: Russian Wikipedia — Шардоне
summary: Classifies Chardonnay as a Burgundian technical white cultivar cultivated in all wine-producing countries and one of the principal international varieties.
notes: It supplies no current Serbian statistics, DWWA arithmetic, Deurić result or regional sensory comparison.

title: Croatian Wikipedia — Chardonnay
summary: Presents Chardonnay as one of the world's best-known wine grapes and summarizes its Pinot × Gouais Blanc parentage.
notes: The article does not support the Serbian rank, 2026 awards or the proposed regional style binary.

title: Vino & Fino — Tri platine i sedam zlata za Srbiju na Dekanteru
summary: Prints all three Serbian Platinum and all seven Gold results: the Gold list contains Tarpoš Chardonnay Extra Brut 2021, Zvonko Bogdan Chardonnay 2022 and Éclater 2018, while La Rem Chardonnay 2023 is Platinum with 97 points.
notes: The result list agrees with Tanjug/Chamber reporting and the official Decanter sources.

title: New Europe Wine Guide — Serbia 2026
provenance: Beth Willard's guide based on 268 named wines from 62 Serbian producers tasted over three days in December 2025
summary: Reports Sauvignon Blanc at 5% of Serbia's end-2024 registered commercial vineyard area and reviews it across several regions. SoviNoa Fumé Blanc 2023 receives 96 and Top White Wine; its note combines lime, nettle, florals and smoky oak. Other northern, Šumadija and southern examples repeatedly mix gooseberry, grass or nettle with peach, pineapple, citrus, apple or tropical fruit.
notes: The guide does not call its tasting a competition or print a Top Sauvignon Blanc category; SoviNoa Fumé Blanc is nevertheless the highest-scoring Sauvignon Blanc in its results.

title: Decanter — International Sauvignon Blanc Day: Award-winning wines to celebrate
provenance: Official Decanter World Wine Awards editorial and result record
summary: Identifies Matijašević SoviNoa Fumé Blanc 2021 as a Serbian Sauvignon Blanc and DWWA 2023 Gold with 95 points, describing peach, gooseberry, grapefruit, citrus, oak, stone fruit and lemongrass together.
notes: This official Decanter result concerns vintage 2021 and 95 points, not the 2023 wine's 96-point New Europe score.

title: Matijašević Vinogradi — SoviNoa Fumé Blanc
summary: Identifies the wine as selected Sauvignon Blanc matured in French oak and describes tropical fruit, ripe peach, citrus, spicy and dried herbs, oak and a long finish.
notes: Producer descriptions are useful for identity and method but do not independently establish a national best-wine rank; the page combines a current product record with earlier award history.

title: Wines of Serbia — Matijašević Vinogradi
provenance: Official Wines of Serbia winery directory
summary: Places Matijašević Vinogradi in Orašac in the Šumadija wine region and lists Sauvignon Blanc among its varieties and SoviNoa and SoviNoa Fumé among its wines.
notes: Directory evidence establishes location and portfolio, not the comparative rank or source of the 96-point score.

title: Wines of Serbia — Vinarija Frug
provenance: Official Wines of Serbia winery directory
summary: Places Vinarija Frug in the Fruška Gora/Srem region and lists Sauvignon Blanc, corroborating current commercial presence in the northern region named by the book.
notes: The directory does not by itself establish a uniform regional flavour profile; wine-level tasting evidence is required for that comparison.

title: Atelje Šapat — Atila Sauvignon Blanc
provenance: Official Fruška Gora producer product specification
summary: Describes a 100% Sauvignon Blanc from the north with lime, gooseberry, vineyard peach, lemongrass, elder, green apple, minerality and fresh acidity, directly showing green, floral and ripe-fruit descriptors in the same regional wine.
notes: One wine cannot define Fruška Gora as a whole, but it contradicts a simple north-green versus south-yellow exclusivity.

title: wein.plus glossary — Sauvignon Blanc
summary: Summarizes the cultivar's broad aromatic range, including grass, herbs, gooseberry and green fruit alongside grapefruit and riper fruit expressions, with climate and ripeness affecting style.
notes: General cultivar evidence supports the plausibility of the descriptors but cannot prove a Serbian regional boundary.

title: Vino.rs — Srpska vina u debelom zlatu
provenance: Serbian specialist report on the New Europe Wine Guide – Serbia 2026
summary: Attributes SoviNoa Fumé Blanc 2023's 96 points to Beth Willard's New Europe Wine Guide and reports the category Top White Wine. It notes Willard's Decanter/DWWA role but does not present the score as a Decanter result.
notes: The assessor's professional connection to Decanter does not turn an independently published guide score into a Decanter score.

title: English Wikipedia — Sauvignon blanc
summary: Describes a global cultivar whose wines may show grassy, bell-pepper, nettle, elderflower and tropical-fruit characters depending on climate and ripeness.
notes: It contains no Matijašević wine, 96-point score, New Europe category or controlled Serbian regional comparison.

title: German Wikipedia — Sauvignon Blanc
summary: Lists gooseberry and green freshly mown grass among characteristic Sauvignon Blanc aromas and records the variety's international distribution, including Serbia.
notes: No Serbian regional split, producer ranking, guide category or Decanter attribution is provided.

title: Hungarian Wikipedia — Sauvignon blanc
summary: Provides only broad international and aromatic cultivar context for Sauvignon Blanc.
notes: It does not support the named Serbian regions, wine, score, assessor or category.

title: Serbian Wikipedia — Совињон блан
summary: Describes Sauvignon Blanc as a dry refreshing wine associated generally with grass, ripe melon, passion fruit and fig.
notes: It supplies no regional Serbian evidence or Matijašević/New Europe/Decanter result.

title: Russian Wikipedia — Совиньон-блан
summary: Lists gooseberry and freshly cut grass, explains a cooler-to-warmer shift toward tropical fruit and includes Serbia among producing countries.
notes: The article does not prove that Serbian southern wines replace rather than combine green notes, nor does it cover SoviNoa's score.

title: Croatian Wikipedia — Sauvignon
summary: Provides general Sauvignon descriptors including green apple, grapefruit, asparagus and wet grass.
notes: It contains no Serbian regional comparison, Matijašević identity, score source or guide category.

title: Vinarija Džervin — current wines and Knjaževac vineyards
summary: Declares a varietal Knjaževac Rhine Riesling 2021, basic Dubravka 2024 as 70% Italian Riesling plus 30% Rhine Riesling, and Dubravka Gold 2024 as 50% Italian Riesling plus 50% Sauvignon Blanc; the estate vineyards lie near Knjaževac at 250–330 metres.
notes: The three product cards distinguish Rhine from Italian Riesling and directly contradict putting Rhine Riesling into the current Gold bottling.

title: Tourism Organisation of Negotin — Wineries
provenance: Official local tourism organisation winery directory
summary: Lists Rhine Riesling among wines or varieties of producers in the Negotin wine area, establishing local presence without a comparative quality ranking against every other white cultivar.
notes: A promotional directory can show current production but cannot by itself establish the cultivar as the region's objectively best white.

title: Wines of Serbia — Vinarija Imperator (& Salaxia)
provenance: Official Wines of Serbia winery directory
summary: Places Imperator's 9.3-hectare vineyard near Erdevik on Fruška Gora and explicitly lists Rhine Riesling among its planted varieties.
notes: One producer proves current presence, not a complete regional area or quality ranking.

title: CEVVIN/Ministry — Rejonizacija vinogradarskih geografskih proizvodnih područja Srbije
provenance: Official national zoning study underlying Serbian viticultural regulation
summary: Includes Rhine Riesling in the documented or permitted assortment of relevant Knjaževac and Negotin subregions and provides regional conditions, but does not rank it above all local white cultivars.
notes: A permitted or recorded assortment is not a comparative blind tasting and gives no «best white» title.

title: Frontiers in Plant Science 2024 — genetic characterization of old Serbian grapevines
provenance: Peer-reviewed original SSR/SNP and historical research
summary: Explicitly identifies Grašac as the local Vojvodina synonym for the white-berried cultivar Welschriesling and discusses its long Serbian history under that identity.
notes: The paper establishes identity; separate catalogue and encyclopedic evidence establishes Welschriesling's non-identity with Rhine Riesling.

title: Wines of Serbia — Grašac Beli: The Serbian White Grape Guide
provenance: Current Wines of Serbia editorial guide citing the 2024 genetic study
summary: States directly that Grašac Beli is Welschriesling/Italian Riesling, is not Rhine Riesling, and should not be mistaken for Rajnski rizling; it treats Grašac as a historically rooted and legitimate Serbian wine identity.
notes: «True Riesling» can disambiguate a label, but the distinct Grašac cultivar should not be framed as fake.

title: Vino.rs — Najbolja vina Srbije 2025: Dubravka Gold 2024
summary: Identifies Dubravka Gold 2024 as a Riesling/Sauvignon Blanc blend and a Best Buy; the abbreviated varietal wording does not distinguish Rhine from Italian Riesling, which the producer's exact declaration resolves as Italian Riesling.
notes: For exact composition, the producer's percentages and explicit cultivar names have priority over the article's shorthand «Riesling».

title: English Wikipedia — Riesling
summary: Defines Rhine-origin Riesling, includes Serbia among countries with significant plantings, and explicitly states that Welschriesling/Italian Riesling is an unrelated cultivar despite the shared name.
notes: It contains no three-region Serbian inventory, Negotin quality ranking or Dubravka product composition.

title: German Wikipedia — Riesling
summary: Identifies Riesling/Rheinriesling as a high-quality late-ripening cultivar and explicitly distinguishes the Rheinriesling name from popular Welschriesling usage.
notes: No Serbian regional distribution, comparative Negotin result or Dubravka blend is supplied.

title: Hungarian Wikipedia — Rajnai rizling
summary: Treats Rajnai rizling as the «real Rhine Riesling», lists Rhine/White Riesling synonyms and gives general origin, viticulture and wine-style information.
notes: It does not establish the three Serbian regions, a Negotin rank or a Džervin recipe.

title: Serbian Wikipedia — Ризлинг
summary: Identifies Riesling as a Rhine-origin German white cultivar also known as Rajnski rizling and notes its popularity in Serbia; the linked Graševina article separately says Graševina/Italian Riesling is unrelated.
notes: It contains no Knjaževac–Negotin–Fruška inventory, quality comparison or Dubravka formula.

title: Russian Wikipedia — Рислинг and Вельшрислинг
summary: States explicitly that Welschriesling is unrelated to Riesling despite the similar name; the Riesling article supplies the separate international cultivar profile.
notes: Neither article provides the local Serbian regional ranking or Dubravka label evidence.

title: Croatian Wikipedia — Graševina
summary: Lists Graševina's Welschriesling, Riesling Italico and related synonyms and describes it as its own white cultivar and wine tradition.
notes: The page is sparse and does not itself state the genetic nonrelationship, so stronger scientific and English/Russian references control that point.

title: UC Davis Foundation Plant Services — Pinot blanc
provenance: University grape variety registry using international catalogue nomenclature
summary: Lists Burgundac Beli among the documented synonyms of Pinot Blanc.
notes: The local Serbian word order Beli burgundac is independently used in Serbian wine references and English Wikipedia.

title: UC Davis Foundation Plant Services — Pinot gris
provenance: University grape variety registry using VIVC-linked synonym data
summary: Lists Burgundac Sivi and Sivi Pinot among the synonyms of Pinot Gris, alongside Pinot Grigio and other international names.
notes: The synonym record proves cultivar identity, not a particular Serbian vineyard share or style.

title: Zvonko Bogdan Winery — Pinot Blanc
provenance: Official winery product and vineyard specification
summary: Declares a 100% Pinot Blanc from Palić vineyards and gives four hectares for the wine, directly documenting a substantial named modern Palić block.
notes: The page intermittently returns a gateway error but remains publicly indexed; it does not identify the four hectares' complete soil profile.

title: Zvonko Bogdan Winery — 8 Guitar Players
provenance: Official winery wine and vineyard specification
summary: Lists Chardonnay, Sauvignon Blanc, Pinot Grigio and Pinot Blanc from Radić, Ludaš and Palić, with 15 hectares assigned to the wine, confirming both Pinot cultivars in a major modern northern Vojvodina portfolio.
notes: The combined locations and area do not allocate hectares or soils separately to each cultivar.

title: Park Palić — Petra Winery
provenance: Official Palić destination and wine-route profile
summary: Places Petra directly beside Lake Palić, records modern plantings beginning in 2009 including Pinot Grigio, and describes the vineyard soil as rich in clay and loam with a humus layer.
notes: The site lies within the broader Subotica wine landscape but is not described as pure sand, demonstrating why exact vineyard soil matters.

title: Wine Routes in Vojvodina Province, Northern Serbia
provenance: Peer-reviewed regional wine-tourism and geography study
summary: Describes the 24,000-hectare Subotica–Horgoš sandland and its vineyards but lists heterogeneous soils including sand, moving sand, clay, chernozem with sand and brown steppe soils.
notes: A regional geomorphological name cannot substitute for a parcel-level soil analysis.

title: New Europe Wine Guide — Serbia 2026
provenance: Beth Willard's current guide and its reproduction of the 2024 Serbian commercial Vineyard Register leaders
summary: The register-derived leading-white list contains Grašac 11%, Chardonnay 9%, Riesling 6% and Sauvignon Blanc 5%, not either white Pinot. The guide nevertheless documents modern Pinot Blanc and Pinot Grigio wines across Serbia, including Vojvodina examples, and scores Zvonko Bogdan Pinot Blanc 2022 at 95.
notes: A 268-wine guide is not a planting census; its register summary is used only to test the unqualified national «foundation» wording.

title: English Wikipedia — Pinot blanc and Pinot gris
summary: The Pinot Blanc article explicitly lists Beli burgundac as a Serbian name; the Pinot Gris article identifies Pinot Grigio as the same globally grown cultivar and emphasizes its broad regional and stylistic range.
notes: The articles contain no Vojvodina share, modern Serbian planting hierarchy or parcel-level Palić soil evidence.

title: German Wikipedia — Weißer Burgunder and Pinot gris
summary: Lists Burgundac Beli for Pinot Blanc and Burgundac Sivi for Pinot Gris in the two cultivar articles, and describes both as internationally distributed members of the Pinot family.
notes: No Serbian regional area statistics or Palić soil allocation is present.

title: Hungarian Wikipedia — Fehér burgundi and Szürkebarát
summary: Identifies Fehér burgundi as Pinot Blanc and Szürkebarát/Burgundi szürke as Pinot Gris/Pinot Grigio, providing neighbouring-language Pinot nomenclature and international context.
notes: It does not cover Vojvodina plantings, Palić or Serbian register ranks.

title: Serbian Wikipedia — Пино гри and Виноградарство у Србији
summary: The Pinot Gris article says the cultivar is grown in Serbia under the name Burgundac sivi, while the national viticulture article lists both Burgundac beli and Burgundac sivi among Serbian cultivars.
notes: The corpus gives no current Vojvodina share or evidence that both varieties form the basis of modern Palić plantings.

title: Russian Wikipedia — Пино-блан and Пино-гри
summary: Treats Pinot Blanc and Pinot Gris as distinct white-wine members of the Pinot mutation group and lists Burgundac sivi among Pinot Gris synonyms.
notes: Neither article quantifies Serbian plantings or identifies Palić vineyard soils.

title: Croatian Wikipedia — Pinot bijeli and Pinot sivi
summary: Identifies Pinot bijeli/Pinot Blanc with Burgundac bijeli and maintains separate Pinot sivi material, giving adjacent South Slavic naming context.
notes: It contains no evidence about Vojvodina, the Serbian commercial register or Palić sands.

title: Plantgrape / INRAE–IFV — Semillon
provenance: French national technical catalogue of cultivated vine varieties
summary: Describes Sémillon as capable, under favourable conditions and managed yields, of full-bodied high-quality dry whites with moderate-to-low acidity, barrel ageing potential and liqueur wines.
notes: This is cultivar potential from professional tastings, not evidence that every Serbian bottle has low acidity or waxy texture.

title: Vino Župa — History of Župa
provenance: Long-established regional producer's history and current regional inventory
summary: Lists Sémillon among current Župa plantings and describes the post-WWII cooperative setting from which Vino Župa emerged.
notes: It does not date Župa's first Sémillon planting or trace a present parcel to a Yugoslav-era vineyard.

title: Vinarija Raj — Zenit
summary: Places the winery at Rajac in Negotinska Krajina and presents Zenit as a varietal Sémillon, calling the cultivar rare in Serbia and available at only a few other wineries; an archival 2017 vintage is also noted.
notes: The page does not publish acidity, full technical composition beyond the varietal wording, vineyard age or national label counts.

title: Vinarija Frunza Aglaja — vineyards and Sauvignon & Semillon
provenance: Official Negotin winery vineyard and wine declarations
summary: States that Sauvignon Blanc and Sémillon grow in the Smedovac vineyard of the Rajac area and identifies Aglaja Sauvignon & Semillon as a structured, intensely fresh citrus wine with a mineral finish.
notes: No percentages, vintage, analytical acidity or separate Sémillon sensory profile are published on the landing page.

title: Vinarija Eden — estate vineyard and Sémillon 2018
provenance: Official Šumadija producer site and linked Sémillon technical card
summary: Dates the seven-hectare estate vineyard and its Sémillon to 2014–2015 and documents a sold-out 100% Sémillon 2018 naturally sweet wine, 10.5% alcohol and inox ageing, described through ripe fig, concentration, balance, full body and sweetness.
notes: An archived sweet half-bottle cannot establish the current national balance of varietal and blended Sémillon.

title: Časopis Vino — Suveren na vinskom tronu
provenance: Serbian specialist historical feature on the royal Oplenac vineyard
summary: Includes Sémillon among the French and German cultivars planted for the royal Oplenac wine programme in the late 1920s and records its use with Sauvignon Blanc in Oplenka.
notes: This is a secondary historical account rather than a parcel ledger, and it does not prove continuity into a current vineyard.

title: English Wikipedia — Sémillon
summary: Describes Sémillon as producing dry and sweet wines, generally heavy with low acidity and an oily texture, and documents both blended and varietal international styles.
notes: Serbia is not treated, so the article cannot establish Župa/Negotin history or national blend frequency.

title: German Wikipedia — Sémillon
summary: Describes powerful, long-lived dry and sweet wines and the common Bordeaux blend with Sauvignon Blanc and Muscadelle, while also recognising dry varietal use.
notes: It lists no Serbian regions, history, current products or production ratio.

title: Hungarian Wikipedia — search: Sémillon
summary: No dedicated Hungarian Sémillon article was found; broader grape and regional pages only identify it as an international white variety.
notes: The corpus contributes no evidence for the Serbian locations, history, style or frequency claim.

title: Serbian Wikipedia — Семијон
summary: Gives general French origin and honey, lemon and lime descriptors and names major foreign countries of cultivation, but does not mention Serbian vineyards despite being the local-language article.
notes: Its sweet-tasting generalisation does not fit all dry or blended Serbian wines and does not verify the book's regional assertions.

title: Russian Wikipedia — Семильон
summary: Provides general ampelography, international distribution and one Crimean varietal example, illustrating that Sémillon can be bottled varietally.
notes: It contains no Župa, Negotin, Yugoslav history or national blend-versus-varietal denominator.

title: Croatian Wikipedia — search: Semillon
summary: No dedicated Croatian Semillon article or Serbian regional material was found in the requested corpus.
notes: The absence supplies no positive or negative evidence about Serbian cultivation or wine style.

title: Plantgrape / INRAE–IFV — Cabernet-Sauvignon
provenance: French national technical catalogue of cultivated vine varieties
summary: States that properly mature Cabernet Sauvignon produces deep-coloured wines with an important tannic structure, ageing and wood-maturation capacity, while vegetal aromas recede as maturity advances.
notes: It does not provide Serbian regional distribution or support an invariant blackcurrant–cedar–tobacco profile.

title: CEVVIN — Kaberne sovinjon
provenance: Serbian Centre for Viticulture and Winemaking cultivar inventory
summary: Says Cabernet is grown throughout Serbia, ranks third by commercial vineyard area and has its largest regional areas in Tri Morave, Srem and Šumadija; it also describes young wines as coarse and the cultivar as sugar-accumulating and suitable for wood ageing.
notes: The page does not publish exact regional hectares or a snapshot year, but its explicit top-three hierarchy contradicts an area-based Negotin-first reading.

title: Ministry of Agriculture of Serbia — Wine Treasure of Serbia: Negotinska Krajina
provenance: Official Serbian protected-origin regional guide, English text edition
summary: Characterises Negotinska Krajina reds as extracted and higher-to-high in alcohol while fresh nights preserve moderate acids, aromatic complexity and colour, and describes the region's terrain, Danube/Timok influence and porous soils.
notes: This PDO-level profile does not call Cabernet the leading variety or every parcel ideal, and it does not define sensory overripeness.

title: Danas — Professor Aleksandar Petrović on Serbia's wine map
provenance: 9 April 2025 direct interview with University of Belgrade associate professor Aleksandar Petrović
summary: Petrović explicitly says Negotinska Krajina has exceptional soil and climate for black cultivars and is ideal for Cabernet Sauvignon, Cabernet Franc, Merlot and Gamay.
notes: The statement is an expert assessment, not a comparative field trial, and it applies to four cultivars rather than Cabernet alone.

title: NIN — Serbian wine map: Aleksandar Petrović on Negotin
provenance: 18 June 2025 direct interview with Aleksandar Petrović
summary: Petrović calls the Negotin area a recognisable terroir and describes Rajačke Pimnice, Rogljevo, Negotin and Mihajlovac as a zone of good, full, rounded Cabernet, Gamay and Začinak.
notes: The interview establishes his view but contains no hectare comparison and does not use «ideal» in this later passage.

title: Decanter World Wine Awards — Matalj Kremen Kamen 2021
provenance: Official searchable DWWA 2026 result and judges' note
summary: Records 97 points and Platinum for Matalj Kremen Kamen 2021 and describes blackberry, blackcurrant, plum, cedar, coffee-oak, earthy and herbal tones with complexity and balance.
notes: One competition result demonstrates a successful wine, not the objective ideality of all Negotinska Krajina for Cabernet.

title: New Europe Wine Guide — Serbia 2026
summary: Scores Kremen Kamen 2021 at 96 and describes it as pure, precise, elegant and not overworked, while other Serbian Cabernets in the same guide range from bright and balanced to jammy, very ripe, overtly sweet-fruited, oxidised and 15–15.5% alcohol.
notes: The sampled guide is not a census, but it directly disproves a uniform Serbian sensory rule.

title: English Wikipedia — Cabernet Sauvignon
summary: Describes Cabernet as dense, dark and tannic, with blackcurrant and temperature-dependent green, ripe and jammy profiles; tobacco, cedar and cigar-box notes may develop with region, oak and age.
notes: No Serbian region, Petrović interview, Kremen wine or DWWA 2026 result is included.

title: German Wikipedia — Cabernet Sauvignon
summary: Highlights cassis, sometimes cedar, concentrated fruit, tannin and acidity, and explains how wood ageing changes and softens the wine.
notes: It contains no Serbian distribution hierarchy, eastern ripeness rule, expert attribution or award record.

title: Hungarian Wikipedia — Cabernet sauvignon
summary: Identifies Cabernet Sauvignon as one of the world's best-known and most widely planted red cultivars and gives broad Bordeaux-blend context.
notes: The article does not verify Negotin priority, sensory claims about Serbia, Petrović or Kremen.

title: Serbian Wikipedia — Каберне совињон
summary: Provides a short general account of Cabernet's global popularity, late ripening, thick skin, French origin and common blends with Merlot and Cabernet Franc.
notes: It does not mention Serbian regions or any of the named expert and competition evidence.

title: Russian Wikipedia — Каберне-совиньон
summary: Describes full body, high astringency and tannin, ripe blackcurrant, under-ripe herbal notes and barrel-age vanilla, smoke, leather, cedar and cigar-box notes.
notes: It supplies no Serbia-specific distribution, Kremen result or Petrović attribution.

title: Croatian Wikipedia — Cabernet Sauvignon
summary: Briefly describes pronounced blackcurrant aroma, dark colour and a full dry wine, but gives no Serbian regional evidence.
notes: The page itself flags an unconfirmed reused-source permission and is not relied on for disputed local claims.

title: Plantgrape / INRAE–IFV — Merlot
provenance: French national technical catalogue of cultivated vine varieties
summary: Describes Merlot as round, powerful, full-bodied and structured, rich in alcohol and colour, relatively low in acidity and bearing rather supple tannins; it also notes clay-limestone adaptation and sensitivity to intense drought.
notes: It defines cultivar potential, not a Serbian average or a north–south latitude rule, and does not specify plum or cherry aromas in its general technological profile.

title: CEVVIN — Merlo
provenance: Serbian Centre for Viticulture and Winemaking cultivar inventory
summary: Says Merlot occupies very significant areas across Serbia, ranks second among all cultivars in commercial vineyards, and has its largest areas in Tri Morave, Srem and Leskovac; its largest altitude band is 300–400 m.
notes: Because Grašac is explicitly first and Cabernet Sauvignon third, Merlot is the leading red by this area ranking; the page publishes no north–south sensory comparison or snapshot year.

title: New Europe Wine Guide — Serbia 2026
provenance: Beth Willard's independent 268-wine Serbia tasting and summary of the 2024 Serbian vineyard register
summary: Reports Merlot at 11% of registered vineyard area, ahead of Cabernet Sauvignon at 9% and Prokupac at 5%; its multi-region tastings repeatedly find plum and red berries but span supple to firm tannins, fresh to jammy fruit and 13.5–15.5% alcohol, and score Zvonko Bogdan Merlot 2023 at 94.
notes: The tasting set is broad but not a random or matched regional sample, so it cannot establish a national north–south gradient; its 94 is separate from the DWWA 95.

title: Decanter World Wine Awards 2025 — Zvonko Bogdan Merlot 2023
summary: Records the 2023 Merlot from Zvonko Bogdan as a 95-point Gold wine and provides the competition tasting note.
notes: This is a competition result, not evidence that all northern Serbian Merlot shares its profile.

title: Decanter — Celebrating Serbian excellence at DWWA 2025
provenance: 8 September 2025 Decanter editorial selection reproducing DWWA judges' notes
summary: Identifies Zvonko Bogdan Merlot 2023 from Palić/Subotica at 95 points and describes ripe blackberry, cassis, tobacco, cedar, deep concentration, inky tannin and mouth-watering acidity at 14% alcohol.
notes: It is another publication of the same DWWA judgment, not independent confirmation of the exact score; the profile is notably more concentrated than the book's simple soft-northern stereotype.

title: English Wikipedia — Merlot
summary: Describes Merlot's softness and fleshiness, medium tannin, plum and cherry families, and contrasts fresher earlier-picked styles with full-bodied, high-alcohol, velvety late-picked styles.
notes: It contains no Serbian planted-area ranking, north–south comparison, Zvonko Bogdan wine or DWWA 2025 result.

title: German Wikipedia — Merlot
summary: Describes fleshy Merlot wines as generally lower in tannin and acidity than Cabernet Sauvignon and higher in alcohol, while giving Bordeaux history and general cultivation context.
notes: It does not verify Serbian prevalence, the claimed latitude gradient or the named award.

title: Hungarian Wikipedia — Merlot
summary: Identifies Merlot as a globally known major red wine cultivar of French and Bordeaux origin and gives broad international context.
notes: No Serbian distribution, sensory sample, north–south comparison or DWWA result is provided.

title: Serbian Wikipedia — Мерлот
summary: Provides a short general account of the dark-blue grape, blueberry and mint traces, Bordeaux blending role and historical global area.
notes: Despite being the local-language article, it gives no Serbian vineyard rank, regional style pattern or Zvonko Bogdan award.

title: Russian Wikipedia — Мерло
summary: Gives French/Bordeaux origin and broad historical distribution, including Merlot's former global planting leadership.
notes: It contains no evidence for Serbia's current ranking, sensory generalisation, latitude gradient or the DWWA result.

title: Croatian Wikipedia — Merlot
summary: Briefly associates Merlot with blackcurrant and plum and calls it drinkable, neither acidic nor astringent.
notes: The terse article offers no sourcing visible in the extracted text and no Serbian regional or award evidence, so it is not relied on for disputed local claims.

title: CEVVIN — Rejonizacija vinogradarskih geografskih proizvodnih područja Srbije
summary: Documents the vineyard geography, relief, climate context and cultivar assortment of Serbian regions, including mountain-framed Knjaževac and the Šumadija/Oplenac area; it provides the strongest regional framework for interpreting Pinot Noir presence and climate suitability.
notes: Regional zoning supports presence and environmental context but does not rank the quality of Pinot Noir or establish a food-pairing rule.

title: Vino.rs — Vinski region Knjaževac
summary: Describes Knjaževac's vineyard landscape, elevation, surrounding mountains, climate and modern producers, and includes Pinot Noir among grapes associated with the region.
notes: Useful secondary regional synthesis, but not a controlled climate comparison or quality census.

title: Vinarija Džervin — Nijansa
summary: Lists Nijansa 2024 as a dry Knjaževac rosé made from 100% Pinot Noir and recommends appetisers, pasta, fish and grilled dishes.
notes: Confirms a current varietal Pinot Noir wine in Knjaževac, but it is rosé rather than the unstated red style implied by the surrounding profile.

title: Vinarija Džervin — Romansa Gold
summary: Lists Romansa Gold 2024 as a Knjaževac rosé blend of 50% Pinot Noir and 50% Muscat Hamburg and recommends prosciutto, pasta, chicken salads and roasts.
notes: Supports a poultry recommendation for one Pinot-based local blend, not mushrooms and not a varietal red Pinot Noir profile.

title: Aleksandrović — Trijumf Noir
summary: Identifies Trijumf Noir as 100% Pinot Noir from the Bokanja site on Oplenac in Šumadija and describes its fruit, silky tannins and freshness; recommended dishes include duck breast and mushroom risotto.
notes: Strong evidence for one named wine and its producer's serving advice, but producer copy cannot establish regional superiority.

title: New Europe Wine Guide — Serbia 2026 Final Report
provenance: Independent current tasting guide covering 268 Serbian wines
summary: Reviews Šumadija Pinot Noirs including Legat 1903 Pinot Noir 2023 and Lastar Sofijin Izbor Pinot Noir 2023, both scored 89, alongside Pinot Noirs from other Serbian regions.
notes: Demonstrates credible regional examples but neither an exceptional national ranking nor the undefined comparative idea of 'unexpectedly well'.

title: English Wikipedia — Pinot noir
summary: Places Pinot Noir mainly in cooler climates, lists Serbia among countries where it is planted and outlines its thin skin, relatively light body and climate-sensitive aroma profile.
notes: It gives no evidence for Oplenac or Knjaževac quality, no Serbian subregional comparison and no local food-pairing rule.

title: German Wikipedia — Pinot noir
summary: Describes Pinot Noir as demanding in site and soil, associated with cooler wine climates, and reports 633 hectares in Serbia in the cited 2016 planting data.
notes: National area data do not identify Oplenac or Knjaževac, measure regional quality or support the pairing sentence.

title: Hungarian Wikipedia — Pinot noir
summary: Provides general cultivar background and international distribution for Pinot Noir.
notes: No usable evidence was found for either Serbian subregion, a quality comparison or the proposed food pairing.

title: Serbian Wikipedia — Пино ноар
summary: Describes Pinot Noir's thin skin, light body, early ripening, terroir sensitivity and greater suitability to cooler conditions than to very hot, dry climates.
notes: The article contains no Oplenac or Knjaževac evidence and no local quality or pairing comparison.

title: Russian Wikipedia — Пино-нуар
summary: Associates Pinot Noir with moderately cool climates, rapid ripening in warm sites, relatively light structure and marked terroir sensitivity.
notes: It does not discuss Serbian subregions, local quality or a poultry-and-mushroom pairing.

title: Croatian Wikipedia — Pinot crni
summary: Gives general notes on thin skins, lighter body, early ripening, heat sensitivity and terroir dependence.
notes: The page carries a source/copying warning and supplies no Serbian regional or pairing evidence, so it is not relied on for the disputed local assertions.

title: VIVC 1459 — BLAUFRAENKISCH
provenance: Vitis International Variety Catalogue, Julius Kühn-Institut
summary: Records BLAUFRAENKISCH as the prime name for VIVC 1459 and includes Frankovka, Kékfrankos and Limberger forms among its extensive synonym set.
notes: VIVC resolves identity, not Serbian regional distribution, wine style or the Verkat award.

title: Pravilnik o rejonizaciji — permitted red cultivars in Serbian vineyard areas
provenance: Službeni glasnik RS 18/2024 consolidated cultivar table
summary: Lists Limberger (Frankovka) within the regulated Serbian red-cultivar framework, including Fruškogorsko vinogorje, and supplies the official regional naming context.
notes: Legal permission does not quantify planted area, prove a typical sensory profile or establish an award.

title: Danch & Granger — Maurer Winery, Szabadka and Fruška Gora, Serbia
provenance: Current specialist importer profile with producer technical data
summary: Documents Kékfrankos among Maurer's Subotica plantings and a 2022 varietal Kékfrankos sourced from Fruška Gora; also describes a Kékfrankos-led local blend as light and refreshing and publishes acidity values for the varietal wine.
notes: One producer working both zones proves presence but cannot measure the cultivar's total regional area or define a Serbian average style.

title: Vinarija Verkat — FranFrankovka 2022
summary: Identifies the Fruška Gora wine as 85% Frankovka and 15% Cabernet Franc, credits Frankovka with freshness and Cabernet Franc with body and structure, and describes red berries, spice, green pepper and twelve months in Hungarian oak.
notes: The current producer page is for 2022, while the vino.rs award names 2023; it confirms the label's established blend design but the vintage-specific award remains separately sourced.

title: Vino.rs — Najbolja vina Srbije 2025: Godina velikih tržišnih izazova
summary: Places FRANKOVKA 2023 VERKAT in the Best Buy category for red wines from international cultivars and identifies Verkat as a young winery from Čerević on Fruška Gora.
notes: This is one publication's editorial price-to-quality selection, not an official medal or cross-publication consensus.

title: English Wikipedia — Blaufränkisch
summary: Recognises Frankovka as the Serbian name of Blaufränkisch, places most Serbian plantings in Vojvodina and describes dark cherry and berry fruit, spice, medium tannin and sometimes very good acidity, with style variation by region and yield.
notes: It does not identify the two Serbian subregions precisely or mention Verkat and its 2025 selection.

title: German Wikipedia — Blaufränkisch
summary: Links Blaufränkisch with Lemberger/Limberger, lists Frankovka and Kékfrankos among synonyms and explains that harvest and élevage can yield either light fruity or powerful tannic wines with cherry and berry character.
notes: No Serbian regional distribution or Verkat award evidence is provided.

title: Hungarian Wikipedia — Kékfrankos
summary: Provides the Hungarian Kékfrankos identity and Central European cultivar context, including generally coloured, acidic and tannic red-wine potential.
notes: It contains no direct evidence for Fruška Gora, Subotica or the vino.rs selection.

title: Serbian Wikipedia search — Франковка / Блауфранкиш
summary: No dedicated Serbian cultivar article was found; scattered winery and wine articles mention Frankovka in Serbian portfolios but do not supply a reliable synonym record, representative style or the Verkat award.
notes: Scattered mentions support only local presence and are superseded by VIVC, regulation and current producer evidence.

title: Russian Wikipedia — Блауфранкиш
summary: Describes Blaufränkisch/Kékfrankos/Lemberger as a Central and Eastern European red cultivar with dark berries, cherry, spice, pronounced acidity and tannin that vary with harvest, maceration and barrel ageing.
notes: The article does not document Serbian subregions or the Verkat wine and award.

title: Croatian Wikipedia — Frankovka
summary: Presents Frankovka as a red cultivar in the regional viticultural context and supplies limited general background.
notes: The short article does not establish the Serbian locations, a medium-density norm or the vino.rs award.

title: VIVC 4377 — GAMAY NOIR
provenance: Vitis International Variety Catalogue, Julius Kühn-Institut
summary: Records GAMAY NOIR as the prime name for VIVC 4377 and includes Game, Game Crni, Gamay Crni and related forms in the synonym set.
notes: VIVC resolves identity, not Serbian planting chronology, regional area or wine style.

title: CEVVIN — Game
provenance: Centre for Viticulture and Winemaking, Serbia
summary: Identifies Game with Gamay/Gamay noir, states that it has significant area in Negotinska Krajina, ranks it 27th by Serbian commercial vineyard area and names Tri Morave, Negotinska Krajina and Toplica as its largest zones. It describes red wine with a pleasant aroma and harmonious taste.
notes: The page gives no 1960s planting date, no producer census and no evidence that light body is the regional norm.

title: NIN — Vinska mapa Srbije: Negotinska krajina
provenance: NIN regional feature, 12 April 2026, with named local and university sources
summary: Lists Gamay among Negotinska Krajina's most represented international cultivars, records it in the current Bukovo monastery vineyard and quotes viticulture professor Aleksandar Petrović describing the region's Cabernet, Gamay and Začinak wines as good, full and rounded.
notes: The feature is not a cultivar-area census and does not date Gamay planting to the 1960s; the sensory judgment is attributed expert opinion.

title: Vinarija Raj — Game and Game 2017
provenance: Current winery portfolio and technical descriptions, Rajac, Negotin
summary: Contrasts generally light French Gamay with a Negotinska Krajina expression described as fuller-bodied, more aromatic and longer-lived. The Game 2017 page says its fruit came from vineyards over forty years old in the Rogljevo-Rajac zone and retained freshness alongside fuller body and ageing potential.
notes: One producer cannot define the regional average; «over forty years» has no precise planting year and does not prove a 1960s start or continuous regional cultivation.

title: Tourism Organisation of Negotin — Vinarije
provenance: Official municipal tourism directory of Negotin wineries
summary: Calls Gamay one of the renowned red wines of the Krajina and lists numerous local uses, including Matalj Dušica rosé, Ivanović's Gamay-Začinak blend, Krajina-Rajac Gamay, Janucić Vulkan, and Dajić Game and Game barrique.
notes: The directory mixes current and legacy portfolio descriptions and promotional claims; its reference to pre-phylloxera Gamay is too ambiguous to establish a planting chronology.

title: Vin de France — Gamay Noir grape variety
provenance: Vin De France national varietal information portal
summary: Describes predominantly fruity Gamay aromas including raspberry, wild strawberry, blackberry and black cherry, with refreshing acidity and little tannin in common whole-bunch styles; it also notes that the wines can be rich and that vinification changes the profile.
notes: A French general profile cannot establish the usual body of Negotinska Krajina Gamay.

title: English Wikipedia — Gamay
summary: Identifies Gamay Noir à Jus Blanc as VIVC 4377 and describes the wines as typically light-bodied and fruity, with strawberry and raspberry in youthful carbonic-maceration styles and fuller, ageable versions from other methods and sites.
notes: The article contains no Negotinska Krajina distribution or planting-date evidence.

title: German Wikipedia — Gamay
summary: Lists Game and Game Crni among Gamay synonyms and describes refreshing light wines with raspberry and cherry aromas alongside more substantial, high-quality cru wines capable of long ageing.
notes: No Serbian regional distribution or 1960s chronology is supplied.

title: Hungarian Wikipedia — Beaujolais, Gamay section
provenance: Requested Hungarian Wikipedia cultivar corpus; no dedicated current Gamay article found
summary: Describes young Gamay wine as strongly fruity and raspberry-like and distinguishes lighter, fruitier styles from more structured and complex examples by site.
notes: The page incorrectly calls Gamay a Pinot Noir variant and gives weak historical claims, so it is not relied on for cultivar identity, origin or Serbian chronology.

title: Serbian Wikipedia — Кључко виногорје
provenance: Requested Serbian Wikipedia corpus, regional page citing Serbian ministry figures
summary: Lists 0.2717 hectares of Gamay, 0.50% of vineyard area, in Ključko vinogorje within the Krajina subregion, providing direct though small and historically dated evidence of local planting.
notes: The underlying table is old and covers one small vinogorje, not all Negotinska Krajina; it supplies neither a 1960s date nor sensory evidence.

title: Russian Wikipedia — Гаме
summary: Identifies Gamay as VIVC 4377 and gives a general wine profile of high acidity, low tannin, light colour and bright fruit aroma.
notes: The article has no Serbian regional distribution, chronology or local style comparison.

title: Croatian Wikipedia — Borgonja (Gamay)
summary: Equates Borgonja with Gamay Noir à Jus Blanc, gives the Pinot and Gouais Blanc parentage, and offers only a generic harmonious-wine description.
notes: The page carries an unconfirmed permissions warning and unsupported historical claims, so it is not relied on for Serbian presence, chronology or style.

title: VIVC 12371 — TEROLDEGO
provenance: Vitis International Variety Catalogue, Julius Kühn-Institut
summary: Records TEROLDEGO as the prime name for VIVC 12371, a black Vitis vinifera wine grape with Italy as its country or region of origin.
notes: VIVC does not prove a precise Trentino birthplace, quantify present global rarity or document the Šapat vineyard.

title: MASAF Registro Nazionale delle Varietà di Vite — Teroldego N.
provenance: Italian Ministry of Agriculture national vine-variety register
summary: Registers Teroldego N. under national code 232 and links recognised clonal material to Trentino institutions and sites including Mezzocorona and Mezzolombardo.
notes: The registry establishes official Italian identity and Trentino technical context, not a complete worldwide planting distribution.

title: Serbian Ministry of Agriculture — Register of recognised plant varieties, Teroldego
provenance: Ministry of Agriculture, Forestry and Water Management, recognised-variety register
summary: Includes Teroldego and registered clone SMA 138 in Serbia, providing official evidence that the rare Italian cultivar is recognised in the national planting-material framework.
notes: Recognition of a cultivar and clone does not identify Šapat's planting material, vineyard area or all Serbian growers.

title: Atelje vina Šapat — Winery, vineyards and Terol
provenance: Current official winery and vineyard page
summary: Locates the complex at Novi Slankamen and the vineyards in Slankamenački Vinogradi; lists Teroldego, Blaufränkisch and Merlot in more than twelve hectares; describes a mainly southern slope at 210–235 metres, thin chernozem over deep lime-bearing loess and Danube views; and presents Terol 2022 as a 100% Teroldego wine.
notes: The page groups cultivars at estate level but does not map parcels or prove immediately adjacent rows. Producer claims about Trentino importance and wine quality need independent support.

title: Vino.rs — Premijere vrhunskih crvenih vina Šapat
summary: Identifies Terol 2022 as a rare Serbian varietal Teroldego from Šapat, reports fruit from the sunny southern exposure above Slankamen and dates the relevant estate vineyards to 2011–2012.
notes: The report calls the wine unique on the Serbian scene but is not a national vineyard census. Its bottle-count details differ from the current producer page and are not used here.

title: English Wikipedia — Teroldego
summary: Describes Teroldego as a red Italian cultivar grown primarily in Trentino-Alto Adige, centred on Campo Rotaliano; reports that roughly 96% of production is Italian and notes sparse smaller plantings abroad.
notes: The worldwide percentage relies on a commercial secondary source and the article contains no Serbia, Šapat or Slankamen site evidence.

title: German Wikipedia — Teroldego
summary: Identifies Teroldego as a northern Italian red cultivar from Trentino, concentrated in Campo Rotaliano, with smaller holdings reported in Istria, near Lake Garda, California and New Zealand.
notes: The acreage figure is dated 1999 and the page supplies no Serbian producer, soil or vineyard-layout evidence.

title: Hungarian Wikipedia search — Teroldego
summary: No dedicated Hungarian Teroldego article or relevant material on its Serbian planting was found.
notes: The Hungarian corpus contributes no independent evidence for origin, rarity, Šapat or the Slankamen vineyard setting.

title: Serbian Wikipedia search — Teroldego / Теролдего
summary: No dedicated Serbian Teroldego article or usable Šapat vineyard entry was found.
notes: Current producer, ministry-register and wine-media evidence is therefore required for the Serbian claims.

title: Russian Wikipedia search — Терольдего / Teroldego
summary: No dedicated Russian Teroldego article was found; scattered genetic mentions in other cultivar pages do not address distribution or Serbia.
notes: The Russian corpus supplies no direct support for the book's origin, rarity or Šapat site claims.

title: Croatian Wikipedia search — Teroldego
summary: No dedicated Croatian Teroldego article or relevant Serbian material was found.
notes: The Croatian corpus does not establish Trentino concentration, Serbian rarity, Šapat or vineyard geography.

title: English Wikipedia — Cabernet Franc
summary: Describes Cabernet Franc as lighter than Cabernet Sauvignon and associates it with raspberry, bell pepper, tobacco, cassis and violets, while stressing dependence on region and style.
notes: The article contains no Toplica, Šumadija or Negotin evidence and cannot establish a Serbian national average or planting wave.

title: English Wikipedia — Marselan
summary: Gives the 1961 Cabernet Sauvignon × Grenache crossing, explains that the programme sought productive large-berried vines and initially rejected Marselan for small berries, and describes renewed interest from disease resistance plus deeply coloured aromatic wines with supple tannins.
notes: It contains no Serbian regional map or 2019 parcel table; its breeding-history wording is checked against the French technical catalogue for traits.

title: English Wikipedia — Syrah
summary: Contrasts moderate-climate black pepper, mint and smoked-meat profiles with warmer-climate, softer-tannin and potentially jammier fruit styles, presenting climate and ripeness rather than country labels as key drivers.
notes: No Toplica, Šumadija or Negotin planting evidence and no count of Serbian style prevalence is supplied.

title: German Wikipedia — Cabernet Franc
summary: Characterises Cabernet Franc as less tannic, less astringent and generally less powerful or full-bodied than Cabernet Sauvignon, with varietal aromatic context.
notes: The German page does not establish Serbian regional occurrence, a modern planting wave or a national descriptor frequency.

title: German Wikipedia — Marselan
summary: Confirms the 1961 Cabernet Sauvignon × Grenache crossing and very small berries; it discusses heat and disease robustness and the cultivar's coloured, aromatic, tannic wine potential.
notes: The article's simplified breeding-goal wording differs from the more detailed English and Russian historical account and is not used alone to determine the original programme objective.

title: German Wikipedia — Syrah
summary: Emphasises Syrah's sensitivity to site, ripeness and over-ripeness and describes a broad spicy, dark-fruited style range rather than a fixed national profile.
notes: It provides no Serbian regional distribution or evidence that an old-world style is more frequent nationally.

title: Hungarian Wikipedia — Cabernet franc
summary: Provides broad Cabernet Franc identity, origin and wine context but no Serbian regional, chronological or representative comparative evidence.
notes: The page does not establish the claimed Serbian frequency, national body pattern or complete descriptor set.

title: Hungarian Wikipedia search — Marselan
provenance: Requested Hungarian Wikipedia cultivar corpus search
summary: No dedicated Hungarian Marselan article or usable Serbian material was found.
notes: The Hungarian corpus supplies no origin, breeding-goal, wine-profile, regional or Serbian 2019-statistics evidence for these claims.

title: Hungarian Wikipedia — Syrah
summary: Describes a full, spicy cultivar whose balance and aroma change with ripeness; excessive ripeness can reduce acidity and aromatic definition, while pepperiness can also be linked to under-ripeness.
notes: No Serbian subregion or national old-world-style prevalence is documented.

title: Serbian Wikipedia — Каберне фран
summary: Says Cabernet Franc occurs in Serbia, commonly alongside Cabernet Sauvignon, and describes it as fruitier and more vegetal, with less tannin and often less fullness; raspberry, bell pepper, violet and spice appear among its descriptors.
notes: It supplies no regional map, current planting chronology, graphite note or representative Serbian national sample.

title: Serbian Wikipedia search — Марселан / Marselan
provenance: Requested Serbian Wikipedia cultivar corpus search
summary: No dedicated Serbian Marselan article or usable entry for its origin, traits, wine profile or 2019 area table was found.
notes: Local-language absence makes official French technical and Serbian inventory sources essential for the disputed details.

title: Serbian Wikipedia — Сира (грожђе)
summary: Presents Syrah style as climate-dependent: cooler settings may show blackberry, mint and pepper, while warmer settings can give softer tannin and different ripe-fruit, anise and leather characters.
notes: Despite the language, the article does not map current Serbian plantings or establish an old-world national majority.

title: Russian Wikipedia — Каберне-фран
summary: Provides general cultivar identity and international cultivation context but no useful Serbia-specific regional, chronological or comparative tasting evidence.
notes: It does not independently support the book's Serbian frequency wording or full descriptor list.

title: Russian Wikipedia — Марселан
summary: Confirms the 1961 Cabernet Sauvignon × Grenache crossing and explains that small berries failed the original high-yield, large-berry programme goal before disease resistance revived interest; it also gives dark colour, aromatic intensity and soft tannins.
notes: The page does not document Serbian hectares, parcels or region-by-region planting and is checked against Plantgrape for technical traits.

title: Russian Wikipedia — Сира (виноград)
summary: Lists pepper, violet, smoke and coffee among common Syrah notes and contrasts them with sweeter, riper warm-climate expressions.
notes: The page supports the descriptor vocabulary, not the claim that one style predominates in Serbia or in the three named regions.

title: Croatian Wikipedia — Cabernet franc
summary: The very short page provides only limited Cabernet Franc identity and general wine context and carries a legacy permission warning.
notes: It is not relied on for Serbian geography, chronology, structural comparison or descriptors.

title: Croatian Wikipedia search — Marselan
provenance: Requested Croatian Wikipedia cultivar corpus search
summary: No dedicated Croatian Marselan article or relevant Serbian material was found.
notes: The Croatian corpus supplies no usable origin, breeding-history, style, geography or inventory evidence.

title: Croatian Wikipedia — Syrah
summary: Explicitly warns that Syrah-versus-Shiraz naming does not impose fixed rules and that climate and winemaking produce styles ranging from pepper and violet to riper, jammier expressions.
notes: It contains no current Serbian regional planting evidence or basis for the word «чаще».

title: Plantgrape / INRAE–IFV — Marselan
provenance: French national technical catalogue of cultivated vine varieties
summary: Records the INRA 1961 Cabernet Sauvignon × Grenache crossing, very small bloomed berries, selective disease susceptibility and wines that are coloured, aromatic, full-bodied and structured by supple non-bitter tannins.
notes: It does not call small berries or disease tolerance the original breeding objective and does not state thick skin; it notes low grey-rot and powdery-mildew sensitivity but susceptibility to young-leaf downy mildew and phylloxeric galls.

title: CEVVIN — Vinogradarstvo i vinarstvo Srbije, 2019
provenance: Serbian Centre for Viticulture and Winemaking inventory based on the Vineyard Register snapshot of 1 March 2019
summary: The cultivar table lists Syrah at 34.32 hectares on 56 parcels and Marselan at 20.21 hectares on 24 parcels; the following Župski Bojadiser row carries the number 40.
notes: The table proves the 24-versus-40 correction and historical scale, but does not itself establish a single recent planting wave or assign all national area to the three heading regions.

title: New Europe Wine Guide — Serbia 2026 Final Report
provenance: Beth Willard's independent current tasting guide covering 268 Serbian wines
summary: Documents Šumadija Shiraz and Marselan blends, Serbian Cabernet Franc examples ranging from elegant and lightly grippy to rich and opulent at 16% alcohol, and Syrah styles ranging from lean peppery to juicy modern expressions.
notes: The guide is broad but not a random vineyard census or matched national comparison, so it cannot establish planting chronology, a national Cabernet Franc average or that old-world Syrah is more frequent.

title: Ministry of Agriculture / CEVVIN — Toplički rejon
provenance: Official Serbian viticultural regionalisation study for Toplica
summary: Provides the official Toplica vineyard geography and regional cultivar inventory, including Cabernet Franc and Marselan among documented international red cultivars.
notes: It does not establish one shared new wave for all three cultivars and does not provide clean current Toplica Syrah evidence for this heading.

title: Danas — Aleksandar Petrović on Serbia's wine map
provenance: National newspaper interview with viticulture professor Aleksandar Petrović
summary: Calls Negotinska Krajina suitable for Cabernet Franc and explicitly lists Syrah among cultivars that, in his view, are missing there but could perform well.
notes: Suitability is not proof of planted area, but the explicit absence judgment cautions against reading the group heading as a current Negotin Syrah claim.

title: Prime Restaurant — current Serbian wine list
provenance: Current Belgrade restaurant list naming wine, region and cultivar
summary: Lists Šumadija examples containing Cabernet Franc and a varietal Djokovic Syrah, alongside regional labels from other Serbian zones.
notes: A restaurant list proves market presence for named wines, not vineyard age, planted area or representativeness; Marselan in Šumadija is independently documented by the tasting guide.

title: Decanter World Wine Awards 2026 — Traško Fabulous Cabernet Franc 2022
summary: Records Traško's varietal Fabulous Cabernet Franc 2022 from Krajina, Serbia, at 89 points and supplies a current named eastern-Serbian Cabernet Franc example.
notes: The result establishes one wine and competition attribution, not the age or area of the vineyard or a regional average sensory profile.

title: Decanter World Wine Awards 2026 — Traško Fucking Fabulous Edición Limitada 2021
summary: Records Traško's Fucking Fabulous Edición Limitada 2021 as a red wine from Negotinska Krajina, Serbia, with 88 points and a Bronze award.
notes: The separate current product specification establishes that Marselan forms 22% of the blend; one wine does not determine regional area or generic sensory style.

title: Decanter — Celebrating Serbian excellence at DWWA 2025
provenance: Decanter editorial selection reproducing DWWA judges' notes
summary: Describes Erdevik Stifler's Mom Shiraz 2020 from Fruška Gora as flamboyant, powerful, full, rich and intense at 15.5% alcohol, with ripe fruit, peppery red berries, mocha and spicy oak.
notes: This is a named counterexample to a simple old-world national rule, not evidence that ripe styles predominate.

title: Vins Rhône — Marselan grape variety
provenance: Official Rhône Valley vineyards varietal portal
summary: Describes very small thick-skinned berries, rot resistance, drought sensitivity, intense bluish ripe skins and deeply coloured, fragrant wines with ripe red and black fruit plus supple harmonious tannins.
notes: These are cultivar traits, not proof that small berries, thick skins or resistance were the original 1961 breeding targets.

title: Serbian wine geographical-indication regulation
provenance: Official Serbian regulation reproduced by FAOLEX
summary: Defines Negotinska Krajina, Knjaževac, Toplica and Šumadija as distinct wine regions and recognises Cabernet Franc, Marselan and Syrah among cultivar names usable in the national wine framework.
notes: National recognition does not prove that each cultivar is planted in each named region; in particular Potrkanje/Knjaževac evidence must not be silently reassigned to Negotin.

title: Wine Explorer — Traško Fucking Fabulous 2021
provenance: Current specialist retailer specification for the named Traško wine
summary: Identifies the wine as a Negotinska Krajina 2021 blend of 65% Cabernet Sauvignon, 22% Marselan and 13% Carmenère, aged in French barriques.
notes: The composition corroborates Marselan use in one regional wine; retailer copy is not used for planted area, breeding history or a national sensory norm.

title: English Wikipedia — Rkatsiteli
summary: Identifies a Georgian white cultivar commonly described as ancient, reports Soviet predominance and 18% of Soviet wine production by 1978, lists Serbia among growing countries, and describes high acidity with spicy and floral notes.
notes: It supplies no Župa or Knjaževac parcel age, Serbian quota document, local planting chronology after the 1970s or evidence for almost no new plantings.

title: German Wikipedia — Rkaziteli
summary: Places the white cultivar in Kakheti, calls it historically ancient, describes its former Soviet predominance and later decline, and records smaller 2016 plantings in Serbia among a wider international distribution.
notes: The page does not document Serbian state allocation, planting motives, old-vine hectares, new-planting frequency or the exact Župa and Knjaževac claims.

title: Hungarian Wikipedia — Grúz borok; Rkaciteli search
provenance: Requested Hungarian Wikipedia cultivar corpus and dedicated-article search
summary: Lists Rkaciteli among Georgian white grapes and gives broad Georgian wine-history and qvevri context; no dedicated Hungarian cultivar article with comparable Serbian or sensory detail was found.
notes: It supplies no Serbian geography, introduction mechanism, socialist planting history, agronomy, age structure or exact descriptor evidence.

title: Serbian Wikipedia — Грузијска вина; Виноградарство у Србији
provenance: Requested Serbian Wikipedia cultivar corpus and dedicated-article search
summary: Calls Rkatsiteli Georgia's leading white-wine grape and notes cultivation beyond Georgia in eastern and former Soviet countries; the Serbian viticulture list separately includes the name among cultivars grown in Serbia.
notes: No dedicated Serbian article was found, and the corpus gives no Župa or Knjaževac parcel age, 1970s mechanism, planting motive, new-vine trend or local sensory evidence.

title: Russian Wikipedia — Ркацители
